candidates.name: Page Flags
candidates.tagline: Type a concept and see every book that discusses it, at the exact pages. Books whose text we hold appear as seismograph strips you can riffle. In-copyright books appear as paper flags, coloured by whether you can open that page tonight.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Type a term. Autocomplete covers about 500 precomputed concepts from the reader's fields, each with a hit count: 'Dutch book', 'proper scoring rule', 'reference class', 'base rate', 'Brier score', 'Kelly criterion', 'Cromwell's rule', 'principle of indifference'.
2) Seismograph wall, for books whose full text we have. Each book is one row, ordered by original publication year. A row is a strip of about 200 bins, with chapter ticks, plus printed-page ticks where [Pg N] markers survive. A Web Worker paints term density, and each row ends with its hit total. A dense band is a chapter about the idea; a lone tick is a passing mention.
3) Flag shelf, for scanned books, via Open Library / Internet Archive Search Inside. Search Inside covers in-copyright lending scans without exposing their text. Each book is one spine, with paper flags at heights proportional to scan page ÷ page count. Flag colour is access:
- green: open scan or Gutenberg; opens the BookReader at /page/n{leaf}/search/{term}
- blue: borrowable now
- grey: restricted; snippet only, plus a library or buy route
- white: HathiTrust full view
Hovering a flag shows a keyword-in-context snippet of about 150 characters and the scan page.
4) Two more lanes: an arXiv rack of abstracts that use the term, and a lecture tape of MIT OCW 6.041SC transcript hits at their timestamps.
5) Riffle: scrub along any seismograph row and page-sized cards flip at 30+ fps with the hits highlighted. Click to pin a page, showing its chapter title and line numbers.
6) Sort spines by shelf order (LCC), year, flag density, or 'readable now first'. A false-friends toggle hides hits whose subjects don't fit.
7) Two-term mode: a second term appears in another hue. Blended colour on seismograph rows, and yellow and pink flags side by side, mark where the two ideas are discussed together.
8) A concordance timeline of first-publication years shows when the term entered the book literature. Synonym chips, proposed by Claude and editable, expand modern terms into period ones ('Bayesian' → 'inverse probability'; 'regression to the mean' → 'reversion').
9) 'Make a packet' saves the chosen pages across books and hands them to the Circulation Desk.
candidates.why_clever:
The back-of-book index is the most underrated research tool. Page Flags is one index across hundreds of books, including in-copyright books the reader doesn't own. It works the way HathiTrust and Google Books full-text search do: page locations without the text.
- Where a flag sits tells you, for free, how deep the treatment is.
- The seismograph shows how a whole shelf attends to an idea in one glance, before you open anything.
- The access colour answers the question search engines ignore: can I read that page tonight?
- The core is pure retrieval, so it works on the static wiki with no model.
The reader would reach for it whenever a paper or conversation raises a concept and they want the three best treatments, at the right pages.
candidates.signature_moment:
The reader types 'miracle'.
- Hume's Enquiry erupts in one dense band: Section X, 'Of Miracles'.
- Venn's Logic of Chance shows a cluster late in the book, in ch. XVII, 'Credibility of Extraordinary Stories'.
- Laplace shows one sharp spike, in 'Concerning the Probabilities of Testimonies'.
They add 'testimon' as the blue channel, and all three bands turn purple: three authors across 140 years working the same problem, found in two seconds.
screens: Term entry with autocomplete and hit-count badges
Seismograph wall: books by year, term density, hit totals, chapter ticks
Riffle: scrubbing a row flips page cards with hits highlighted; pinned page

Flag shelf in LC order with access-coloured flags at positional heights, e.g. 'Dutch book' with Earman's Bayes or Bust?, Skyrms's Choice and Chance and Diaconis & Skyrms's Ten Great Ideas About Chance flagged, and three Dutch book-design annuals folded away as false friends
Flag hover card: KWIC snippet, scan page, edition, open/borrow action
Two-term overlay: blended rows and a list of where flags from both terms sit together
Lanes view: book shelf, arXiv rack and lecture tape; concordance timeline
Packet builder handing pages to the Circulation Desk; mobile list with mini flag bars
candidates.data_needed:
Search Inside, precomputed:
- Query openlibrary.org/search/inside.json for about 500 terms. Tested: 'proper scoring rule' returns 97 English books, 'reference class' about 3,400 hits, 'Dutch book' 4,098 hits.
- Store the ia id, title, page_num, availability, and highlight snippets truncated to about 150 characters.
- Cap each term at about 60 books, with one lazy-loaded JSON file per term.
- Join to catalog.json by IA id; 4,864 catalog works have one.

Full texts:
- The 9 in texts/, plus 200-500 public-domain texts from gutenberg.json chosen by class and subject.
- Each with chapter boundaries and [Pg N] page maps.
- Either scanned in a worker or shipped as a binned inverted index.

Other lanes: papers.json abstracts, and the OCW 6.041SC transcript PDFs converted to text with approximate timestamps.
candidates.prior_art:
- Marti Hearst's TileBars (CHI 1995) and Seesoft (Eick et al., 1992).
- HathiTrust full-text search, which gives page numbers without the text (Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, 2014).
- Google Books search-inside, and Internet Archive / Open Library full-text search.
- Cruden's concordance and back-of-book indexes.
- Voyant Tools; Google Ngram Viewer and Bookworm.

New here: one view that joins full-text density strips with page flags for in-copyright books; access status for each page; two-term overlay; and packets that become reading assignments.
candidates.risks:
- Page numbering: page_num is the scan leaf, not the printed page. Label it 'scan p.' and link by BookReader n-index.
- Sparse flags for lending scans: the public API returns one best page per book per query, and the per-item inside.php search is closed for lending items (verified). So books with many flags are mostly open scans.
- HathiTrust: full-text search is Cloudflare-blocked for scripts, so it can't be a bulk source.
- Matching quality: OCR noise, archaic spellings ('to-morrow') and false friends need filtering, and matching is lexical, not semantic.
- Fair use: snippets must stay short.
- Rate limits when precomputing.
- Staleness: availability goes out of date, so show the snapshot date.

usefulness.why: 'Which books treat concept X, at which pages, and can I open that page tonight' is the find-the-right-page and compare-treatments need, met by pure retrieval the reader can trust. Usefulness is capped because Search Inside gives only about one page per lending book and the full-text strips cover mostly pre-1930 books.

novelty.why: It joins TileBars and Seesoft density strips with Search Inside page flags coloured by whether you can read the page tonight, and the two-term 'miracle'/'testimon' overlay is a nice moment. But it is an updated concordance on 30-year-old ideas and existing full-text search.

demo.why: The best fit for one day. The seismograph wall is plain term-density binning over the 9 local texts plus fetched Gutenberg texts, needs no model, works on the static wiki, and is striking within 5 seconds. I verified that Search Inside answers from our machine (about 5 s per query) and that the 'miracle' hits exist in Hume, Venn and Laplace. The flag shelf will be sparse, because lending scans return one best page per book.

candidates.name: Evidence Ledger
candidates.tagline: Read 1,457 papers as evidence, not documents. Every quantitative claim is extracted onto one chart against human baselines, and every paper becomes a likelihood ratio on a proposition you care about, so your posterior moves as you read.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Claims view. Pick a measure family: LLM forecasting accuracy (Brier), calibration of verbalised confidence (ECE), reward-hacking rate, LLM-as-judge agreement with humans, or 'any % improvement'.
- The chart has one mark per claim, not per paper: x is the date, y is the reported value (direction normalised so 'better' is always up), colour is the benchmark (ForecastBench, Metaculus, Polymarket...), and shape is the system type (single LLM, retrieval, ensemble, human crowd, superforecasters).
- Dashed lines show human baselines, such as the superforecaster median.
- Hover shows the abstract sentence with the number highlighted.
2) Comparability guard. Claude extracts metadata for each claim: dataset, horizon, scoring variant, and leakage risk relative to the model's training cutoff.
- A 'comparable only' toggle greys out mismatches and lists the reasons.
- A forest-plot mode groups claims by benchmark.
- No trend line is ever fitted across benchmarks.
3) Proposition view. Write a proposition that can resolve, and set a prior, e.g. 'By end of 2027 an LLM system matches the median superforecaster on ForecastBench', 40%. In-browser BM25 plus theme tags narrow the papers to about 60 candidates. For each paper Claude returns:
- relevant, or 'not this question' with a reason;
- stance;
- the abstract span carrying the evidence, as character offsets the page verifies;
- evidence type (benchmark result, ablation, theory, position paper, survey, self-reported system);
- a proposed likelihood ratio (LR) with a one-line rationale;
- a dependence group (same benchmark, same authors or same data).
4) Ledger. Rows run in date order, like a bank statement.
- Each row has a log-scale LR slider (0.2× to 5×), preset to Claude's proposal and draggable.
- Above the rows, a curve shows the posterior after each paper in publication order: the literature's trajectory.
- Papers in one dependence group are combined through a discount knob, from 'independent' to 'count the group once'.
- Every number carries an 'AI-proposed' badge until the reader touches it. A blind mode hides Claude's proposals until the reader has set their own LRs.
5) Sensitivity. A tornado chart shows which rows move the posterior most, and a scatter compares Claude's LRs with the reader's.
6) What would change my mind. Claude proposes 3 hypothetical studies with their expected LRs (value of information), and the page searches the corpus for any that already exist.
7) Live extraction. Paste a new abstract and a JSON record streams in: {metric, value, interval, baseline, dataset, horizon, direction, quote}. The page string-matches the quote and checks the number against it before the dot animates onto the chart.
8) Ask and export. 'Ask the ledger' answers through a query_ledger tool and leaves the chart filtered to its evidence. Export as CSV with provenance, a Markdown rationale, or a Squiggle snippet.
candidates.why_clever:
A list or summary of 1,457 papers does not say what the literature found, or how much any one paper should matter.
- Exploration moves from documents to the evidence inside them. Scale, direction, base rate and leakage, which are the whole story for a forecasting reader, are encoded on the chart rather than buried in text.
- The reader's own mental model, Bayesian updating, becomes the interface, so a pile of abstracts becomes a belief with a visible audit trail.
- It exposes double counting (five papers on one benchmark) and separates papers about the question from papers merely near it.
- Every point traces back to its sentence.
- Generated stances, spans and LRs appear as proposals in editable controls, never as verdicts, so the reader inspects the model's judgement rather than absorbing it.
candidates.signature_moment:
The reader sets a 40% prior on LLMs reaching superforecaster parity, and rows stream in.
- Abolghasemi et al. 2023 (retail sales; 'LLMs do not consistently outperform humans'): LR 0.8.
- Tan et al. 2024, 'Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?', drops into the 'not this question' tray (numeric series, not judgmental forecasting).
- The AIA Forecaster report (2511.07678) arrives with its span highlighted ('achieves performance equal to human superforecasters' on ForecastBench), a proposed LR of 3.0, and a badge: 'self-reported by the system's builders'.
- Forecast-Dojo (2609.28876) comes in at 1.3.
The posterior jumps to 68%. The reader drags the AIA row down to 1.5 and the curve bends back to 51%. Switching to the Claims view, the AIA dot sits on the dashed superforecaster line, beside a hatched cluster labelled 'possible leakage'.
screens: Measure-family picker with claim counts
Claims time-scatter with baseline lines, benchmark colours and system-type shapes; hover card with highlighted sentence
Comparable-only toggle and forest-plot mode
Proposition setup with resolution criteria, prior slider and suggested propositions
Candidate triage with the 'not this question' tray
Ledger: rows with highlighted spans, evidence badges, LR sliders and dependence colours; posterior trajectory above
Sensitivity tornado and LR scatter; 'what would change my mind' cards
Live extraction drawer with validation ticks; export (CSV, Markdown, Squiggle)
candidates.data_needed:
Papers:
- papers.json: abstracts, themes, dates (CC0). Abstracts alone are thin: 32 mention Brier, 7 ECE, 90 reward hacking, and about 180 contain percentages.
- To widen coverage, fetch arXiv HTML full text at build for about 400 recent papers in the forecasting, scoring-rules, uncertainty, ai-evaluation and alignment themes, and extract results tables and sentences.
- Crossref for DOIs, venues and citation counts.

Indexes and hints: an in-browser BM25 index, plus dependence hints from shared authors and shared benchmark names.

Precomputed:
- The ledger of claims (quotes plus comparability metadata), with a validator pass.
- Ledgers for 4-5 propositions.
- A hand-checked gold set of about 30 claims, so the page can show an extraction-accuracy figure.
candidates.prior_art:
- Evidence synthesis: meta-analysis forest plots; Heuer's Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (CIA, 1999).
- AI research tools: Elicit's extraction tables; Papers with Code leaderboards; scite's supporting and contrasting citations; Consensus Meter.
- Forecasting: ForecastBench's leaderboard; Metaculus and Good Judgment rationales.
- Bayesian tools: Arbital's guide to Bayes' rule; Guesstimate and Squiggle.
- Kialo argument maps.
candidates.risks:
- False precision: LRs read off abstracts are crude, and abstracts overclaim. Use coarse slider ticks, an 'abstract only' badge, and ranges rather than point values.
- Anchoring on Claude's proposed LRs; blind mode addresses this.
- Independence assumptions fail in tight literatures, and the dependence knob is only a heuristic.
- Stance can be misclassified, especially for papers on an adjacent task.
- Extraction errors are mitigated by quote validation and the gold-standard accuracy figure shown on the page.
- Real incomparability makes any cross-benchmark trend misleading.
- The corpus is arXiv only, and the literature moves fast, so date-stamp everything.

usefulness.why: For a forecaster following a fast-moving literature (LLM forecasting, calibration, evals), one-mark-per-claim charts against human baselines, with comparability guards, are a genuine 'understand the field' tool they would revisit. The LR ledger is useful but leans on crude, abstract-only judgements, and the corpus is thin (about 1.4k arXiv abstracts).

novelty.why: Elicit tables, forest plots and leaderboards exist. But treating each paper as an editable likelihood-ratio slider, with a posterior trajectory in publication order, a dependence discount and a blind mode, makes a literature into an auditable Bayesian update. I haven't seen that as an interface, and it fits this reader closely.

demo.why: The ledger mechanics are easy and deterministic: LR sliders, a log-odds posterior trajectory and a tornado chart. Claim extraction over 1,457 abstracts is cheap at build time. The claims scatter will be thin from abstracts alone (about 32 Brier mentions) unless arXiv HTML is fetched. Visually it is a chart and a table, so it is less arresting than the stronger concepts.

candidates.name: The Circulation Desk
candidates.tagline: Paste any reading list and a departures board flips each item to where it can legally be read tonight, totals the cost and hours, and names the one key (a library card, a month of a subscription, a skill) that would open the most doors next.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Intake. Paste anything: a syllabus, a blog post's bibliography, messy notes ('Jaynes prob theory; Sutton Barto; that Neyman scoring-rules paper; Superforecasting'), DOIs, arXiv ids or ISBNs. You can also pick a paper and pull its Crossref references, or import a packet of flagged pages from Page Flags.
2) Matching is deterministic first: regexes for arXiv ids, DOIs and ISBNs, then Fuse.js fuzzy title-and-author matching against catalog.json, gutenberg.json, openstax.json and papers.json. Only leftovers go to Claude, through a find_candidates(text) tool, and Claude must return a local id or 'unresolved', so it cannot invent a book. Each entry becomes an editable call slip with a match-confidence bar. Unresolved items wait in a tray.
3) Departures board. Each item gets one Solari-style row that flips to ranked route chips:
- FREE public domain: Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, LibriVox.
- FREE open access: arXiv, OpenStax, Unpaywall, and a link-checked list of author- and publisher-hosted PDFs.
- BORROW: Internet Archive 1-hour or 14-day loan, via the ia id.
- PRINT-DISABLED ONLY: shown only together with its eligibility rules.
- LIBRARY: Libby or WorldCat, by ISBN.
- SUBSCRIPTION: O'Reilly or Perlego, with a confidence level from a publisher table.
- BUY: a dated used-price band.
- SEARCH-ONLY: HathiTrust page pointers.
Every route carries a 'checked on' date.
4) Hold shelf. The bins become physical piles whose height is total pages ('Free now: 1,640 pages, 16 cm'). A cost meter and an hours meter, at the reader's own pace, sit alongside.
5) Keyring. A drawer holds the keys the reader has.
- Access keys: Open Web (always held), IA account, public library card, subscription, university visitor, interlibrary loan, wallet.
- About 20 skill keys: calculus, linear algebra, measure theory, mathematical statistics, information theory, game theory and so on. Claude tags skill prerequisites for about 1,500 technical works at build time, labelled 'AI-estimated'.
A work's door opens when you hold any one of its access keys and all of its skill keys. Toggling a key sends a ripple of doors opening across the board, and an 'open to you now' counter rolls.
6) Next Key advisor. It ranks the keys you don't hold by wishlist doors opened per dollar or per hour:
- 'free library card: +11 doors'
- 'one month of a subscription: +19 (illustrative)'
- 'measure theory, about 40 h from a free text: opens Billingsley and Durrett, +8'
A cheapest-complete-path optimizer compares options, for example one month of O'Reilly covering four items against buying two used copies.
7) Free shadow. When an item has no free route, a panel lists free material that covers the same ground (a lecture series, the author's papers, OpenStax chapters). Each comes with a coverage note labelled as a judgement.
8) Weekly ledger and exports. The ledger shows what changed since the last visit: newly free, loan now available, new OA version. Inside the artifact this is a dated snapshot. Exports: BibTeX/RIS, a 'tonight' packet of direct links with page anchors, and an ISBN list for interlibrary loan.
candidates.why_clever:
Reading widely is limited less by finding than by getting, because every item sits behind a different door.
- The desk replaces 30 tabs of checking with one batch triage. This puts the catalog/content split to work: the catalog is small and local, and every record already carries all its legal routes ranked by cost.
- Batching supports decisions that per-item lookup can't: subscription break-even, what can start tonight, and which single key unlocks the most.
- The model only touches entries the deterministic matcher can't resolve, and only by choosing among real records.
- It surfaces the saving catalogs miss: textbooks that Open Library marks 'no ebook' but whose authors or publishers host them free.
- Treating prerequisite skills as locks beside access locks matches how a measure-theoretic textbook actually feels.
The reader would open this for every new syllabus, every paper's reference list and every list a colleague sends.
candidates.signature_moment:
The reader pastes a 12-line list from a forecasting reading group, and the rows clack over one at a time.
- Bishop's Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning shows NO EBOOK, then flips to FREE (publisher-hosted PDF).
- Sutton and Barto's Reinforcement Learning goes from NO EBOOK to FREE (authors' site).
- Hastie et al.'s Elements of Statistical Learning goes from BORROW 1 HR to FREE.
- Keynes's A Treatise on Probability is FREE as Gutenberg #32625.
- Superforecasting stays amber (print-disabled only), and its free shadow opens.
The summary bar flips to '9 of 12 readable tonight for $0'. Then the reader toggles the Internet Archive key. A ripple runs across the whole catalog as 2,020 borrowable doors swing open, and the advisor's top card slides up: 'One free library card opens 11 more of your wishlist.'
screens: Intake: paste box with sample lists, arXiv-paper picker, 'import my flags'
Call slips: parsed citations with match confidence, editable fields, unresolved tray
Departures board mid-flip, with a 'readable tonight' filter
Hold shelf: piles with page-height, cost and hours meters
Item detail: every route ranked with check dates, edition notes, HathiTrust search-only link and the free shadow
Keyring drawer and the door ripple after toggling the IA key
Next Key advisor plus cheapest-path and subscription break-even panel
Weekly 'what changed' ledger and export drawer (BibTeX/RIS, tonight packet, ILL ISBN list)
candidates.data_needed:
Embedded data:
- catalog.json: acc (280 public, 2,020 borrowable, 2,325 printdisabled, 2,255 no ebook), ia ids for 4,864 works, pg/se/lv ids, isbn, pp.
- gutenberg.json; openstax.json (84 CC BY textbooks); papers.json (always free).

Build-time routes.json:
- A hand-curated, link-checked list of legal author and publisher PDFs for well-known textbooks.
- HathiTrust Bib API rights (full view vs search-only), by ISBN or OCLC number.
- Unpaywall OA locations and Crossref metadata for DOIs.
- IA availability.
- A publisher-to-subscription table with confidence levels.
- WorldCat and Libby URL patterns.

Also needed:
- Skill tags for about 1,500 QA/Q/HB/T works, from a fixed vocabulary, with confidence.
- A Fuse.js index over titles and authors.
- A date on every route and price.
- The per-viewer keyring and queue, kept in the storage capability (localStorage on the wiki).
candidates.prior_art:
- Single-item OA lookup: Unpaywall, Open Access Button, LibKey Nomad, Lean Library, EndNote Click.
- Library Extension (library availability on bookstore pages); BookFinder; Libby; Zotero's 'Find Available PDF'; OpenURL link resolvers.
- Airline Solari boards.
- Metroidvania lock-and-key design (Super Metroid, Hollow Knight) and Mark Brown's 'Boss Keys'.

New here: batch triage of whole lists across every access channel, including subscriptions and skills; physical totals; a marginal-key advisor; and a weekly re-route.
candidates.risks:
- Legality and link rot: list only legal routes, never shadow libraries, and show check dates.
- Staleness: availability changes (IA lending changed after Hachette v. Internet Archive) and can't be checked live inside the artifact.
- Holdings: library and subscription holdings aren't in our data, so those keys are illustrative and must say so.
- Eligibility: print-disabled access must only be offered to eligible readers.
- Ambiguity: titles like 'Machine Learning' need edition confirmation.
- Prices: they need a live source, so the artifact shows dated estimates.
- Skill tags are LLM-estimated and subjective.
- Crossref reference lists are missing for many papers.

usefulness.why: This hits the most concrete bottleneck, scattered access, at the moment it actually happens: a syllabus or reference list arrives. R01's coverage test (44% of canonical books free, 65% with controlled lending) shows how much hidden free access batch routing would surface. The skill-key and Solari theatrics add little, and holdings and staleness limits mean the core routing board and export carry the value.

novelty.why: Batch legal-access triage is useful logistics, not a new way to explore literature. Single-item versions exist (Unpaywall, LibKey, Library Extension, BookFinder, Zotero). The Solari board and skill-key locks are clever packaging on a familiar job.

demo.why: The core is deterministic: Fuse.js matching, a Solari-style board over the acc/ia fields, and an access-key ripple. The signature items are really in catalog.json with the claimed statuses (Bishop no_ebook, ESL borrowable, Superforecasting printdisabled), so the flips only need an hour of curating legal author PDFs. To fit a day, cut skill keys, the optimizer and the ledger, and label library and subscription keys as illustrative.

candidates.name: The Great Conversation
candidates.tagline: Ask about an idea and Claude stages a conversation across three centuries in which every line is a verified quotation it was never allowed to type. You can lay it out as a timeline score, as parallel polyglot columns, or as books seated around you.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Ask. Type a question ('Will the sun rise tomorrow?', 'How far should testimony move us?', 'Is chance only our ignorance?', 'What is the probability of a single event?') or pick one of about 10 precomputed ideas.
2) Claude searches. It runs an agent loop over the local full texts with page tools:
- search(terms | regex, books) returns hits with line numbers;
- read(book, from, to) returns a window of text;
- context(book, line) returns the chapter title and printed page;
- list_texts.
Claude returns a 'score' as JSON: an ordered list of turns, each {book, lineStart, lineEnd, anchor (a short string that must occur in the span), role: claim | reply | objection | example | number | repair | critique, respondsTo}. It may add editor's notes of at most 25 words. Claude never outputs quotation text.
3) The page verifies. It looks up every pointer, checks that the span exists and contains its anchor, and renders the passage from the file. A counter reads '14 proposed, 12 verified, 2 rejected'. Rejected finds stay visible as crumbled grey fragments.
4) Three layouts of the same score:
- Score: a vertical timeline (1748 at the top, 2026 at the bottom) with one column per author. Turns stream in as they verify, and editor's notes between eras say how the idea mutated.
- Hexapla: six or seven parallel columns ordered by date, with rows aligned by argument move (statement, worked example, objection, repair, modern form). Ruled lines join aligned passages, glosses in the gutters cite paragraph ids, and a diff lens tracks one word ('probability') changing sense across columns.
- Round Table: in three.js or WebXR, each book sits on a lectern around you. Pages turn in a ripple to their passages, the table rotates the speaking book into view, and red threads cross the table between seats that disagree.
5) Arcs. Solid arcs mark text reuse the page detects itself (a rare number or an 8-word shingle shared between books). Dashed arcs mark Claude's inferred 'responds to'.
6) Context. Click any quote for a drawer showing 40 lines either side, the chapter, and the printed page where a [Pg N] marker exists. 'Read from here' opens Gearbox at that place.
7) Carry it forward. Modern voices join without speaking freely:
- In-copyright catalog books appear as sealed columns or silent guests, showing only Search Inside page hits and access routes (Jaynes's Probability Theory; Taleb's The Black Swan, whose turkey descends from Russell's chicken).
- arXiv papers speak only in verified abstract spans.
- MIT OCW 6.041SC can join as a transcript column with timestamps.
8) More tools. 'Find the counter-voice' re-runs selection to find the strongest disagreement. 'Add a witness' drags any Gutenberg book in. Export as an annotated bibliography or a controversy table (question x author x quote x locator).
candidates.why_clever:
A search box returns loose passages, and a summary replaces the passages with its own words.
- Here the LLM does what it is good at: finding, selecting and ordering relevant passages across 1.2 million words.
- It is barred from what it is bad at, reproducing text faithfully, because its output is pointers that the page looks up and checks.
- The reader sees the shape of a 160-year argument in three minutes, and every sentence on screen is primary source.
- The reuse arcs are evidence the model cannot fake.
Each layout earns its place:
- the score shows chronology;
- the hexapla, the oldest scholarly technology for comparing texts, shows how a concept was stated, attacked, repaired and turned into a tool;
- the round table gives each author a fixed seat, so a headset can show seven legible pages at once and the debate gets a geography you remember.
Sealed columns keep the catalog/content split honest: free texts do the explaining, and paid ones get exact pointers.
candidates.signature_moment:
The reader types 'Will the sun rise tomorrow?' and five columns fill from the top:
- Hume (1748): 'That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition...'
- Laplace (1814): 'it is a bet of 1826214 to one that it will rise again to-morrow'.
- Jevons (1874): after a thousand million sunrises, the chance that the sun keeps rising for as long again is 'almost exactly 1/2'.
- Venn (1888), in 'The Rule of Succession', cites the 1,826,214 to 1 and De Morgan's ships with flags, then writes: 'It is hard to take such a rule as this seriously'.
- Russell (1912): 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead'.
A solid arc snaps from Venn back to Laplace, labelled 'verified: same number in both texts'. The page computed that link; the model did not assert it. Switch to the round table, and the same five books are seated around you, with Taleb's closed Black Swan lighting up beside Russell as a silent guest.
screens: Ask: question field, precomputed ideas as chips, corpus strip placing the books on a 1748-1923 timeline
Assembling: author columns appearing, proposed / verified / rejected counter, tool-call ticker
Score: timeline with solid reuse arcs, dashed responds-to arcs, and mutation notes labelled AI
Hexapla: columns aligned by argument move, with gutter glosses and the diff lens on 'probability'
Round Table: lecterns in a ring, page-turn ripple, disagreement threads, silent guests (desktop panorama strip as fallback)
Context drawer with 40 lines either side and 'read from here'
Carry it forward: sealed modern columns with page hits, arXiv abstract spans, lecture column
Audit view: raw JSON score, rejected pointers with reasons, model and corpus version; export
candidates.data_needed:
Texts:
- texts/*.txt: 9 books, about 1.2M words, addressed by line.
- At build time, 100-200 more public-domain texts from gutenberg.json in B, BC, HB, Q and QA (Keynes #32625, Boole #15114, Mill's System of Logic #27942, De Morgan #23100, Bacon #45988, Galton #11562), lazy-loaded per book.

Build:
- A per-book inverted index (term to line numbers), so tool calls return in milliseconds.
- A text-reuse table of rare numbers and 8-word shingles shared across books.
- Chapter boundaries.
- [Pg N] page maps (present in Venn, Jevons and Poincaré).
- About 10 precomputed scores.

Also needed:
- Search Inside hits for the sealed modern witnesses.
- OCW 6.041SC transcripts with timestamps.
- catalog.json and papers.json for modern voices.
- Troika SDF text, so pages are legible in WebXR.
candidates.prior_art:
- Adler's Syntopicon (1952).
- Parallel-text traditions: Origen's Hexapla, the Complutensian Polyglot, variorum editions, the Talmud page, Perseus parallel texts.
- Collation tools: Juxta and the Versioning Machine.
- KWIC concordances.
- Google's Talk to Books (2018).
- Text-reuse detection: passim, TRACER.
- Anthropic's Citations API.
- The cento, a poem made only of other poets' lines.
- Scholarship this makes browsable: Ian Hacking's The Emergence of Probability and Dale's A History of Inverse Probability.
- Immersive Space to Think (Lisle et al., IEEE VR 2021); Heaven's Vault.
candidates.risks:
- Distortion: a quote montage can mislead by omission or by one-sided arrangement. Mitigations are the context drawer, the counter-voice pass, and showing what each author says next.
- Corpus: it is small and mostly 19th-century English, so the value depends on build-time expansion, and the 20th century is sealed.
- Locators: Gutenberg line numbers aren't printed pages. Quote matching must normalise Gutenberg markup (Hume's line has italic underscores).
- Links: verification proves a quote exists, not that a 'responds to' link is right, so those links stay dashed unless the page detects reuse.
- Latency: agent loops take 20-60 s, so stream turns as they verify.
- Editor's notes can smuggle in claims, so keep them short and visually distinct.
- Layout: six columns are cramped below 1200 px; use a swipeable deck on mobile.
- Headset: WebXR text needs SDF rendering, and the table rotates rather than the reader's head, to avoid neck strain.

usefulness.why: The verified-pointer pattern is excellent engineering, but a quote montage over about 200 public-domain, mostly 19th-century books seldom helps this reader choose or locate reading in their modern fields. Its useful core duplicates the Crux Table.

novelty.why: The model may only return line pointers, and the page fetches and checks every quote. That makes a fully verbatim, cross-century debate, a pairing of LLM selection with LLM abstention that Talk to Books (2018) never attempted. The reuse arcs are detected by the page rather than claimed by the model, and the hexapla alignment by argument move is fresh. It overlaps with Crux Table.

demo.why: All five sunrise quotes are in the local texts: Hume at line 695, Laplace 1826214 at line 610, Jevons 'almost exactly 1/2', Venn 'hard to take such a rule', and Russell's chicken. The Venn-to-Laplace reuse arc can also be computed by the page. The Score layout with pointer verification plus 3-5 precomputed conversations is a one-day build; the hexapla and Round Table are stretch goals, and live agent loops are slow.

candidates.name: Gearbox
candidates.tagline: One book, a bet, and five reading speeds. Bet on what each chapter argues, let your surprise set the gear, then riffle, skim, read or study without losing your place, with dog-ears where later books quoted the page.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Open a full text. It can be one of the 9 local Gutenberg books, one of about 30 more fetched at build time (Keynes's Treatise #32625, Mill's System of Logic #27942, Boole #15114, Poincaré's Science and Hypothesis #37157), or your own EPUB/TXT dropped onto the page and parsed in the browser. Each book is segmented into chapters, paragraphs and sentences, with stable pseudo-pages of about 370 words.
2) Fore-edge. The book first appears edge-on, and its page block is a visualization:
- bands for chapters;
- darker bands for numerals, tables and equations;
- a heat map for the active query term;
- dog-ears standing up on pages that later books quote, with provenance on hover ('quoted by N later books, incl. Dale, A History of Inverse Probability').
3) Bet first. For each chapter you see only its title, its section headings and the previous chapter's last paragraph. (Venn's TOC, for example, gives ch. VIII §8 'Is it a strict rule of inference?' and §9 'Or is it a psychological principle?'.)
- Spread 100 points over four candidate main claims. One is true and anchored to a quote. Three are distractors, checked to be unsupported by the chapter and matched in length and style.
- The reveal shows your log score in bits, the correct claim, and the decisive passage highlighted.
- After a handful of bets, the spine shades by surprise and each chapter gets a recommended gear.
- Chapters you aced can drill down to bets on individual sections.
4) Five gears on one lever (keys 1-5, or a thumb slider on a phone). Shifting folds and unfolds paragraphs around the sentence under the reading line, so you never lose your place.
- 1, Riffle: hold Space and pages flip as thumbnails at about 8 per second. Each shows only headings, defined terms, numbers and a 'glimpse line', the page's most distinctive sentence. 'Speed bumps' slow the riffle to about 1 page per second on pages dense in your query terms.
- 2, Skim: extractive only, about 10% of the words (first sentences, definitional sentences, sentences with numbers). The rest shrinks to clickable hairlines, and each paragraph has a bar showing how much new information it adds.
- 3, Inspect: an Adler inspectional card for each chapter (what kind of chapter it is, the question it answers, key terms, its unity in one sentence), above a 25% extractive digest.
- 4, Read: the full text, with a margin minimap.
- 5, Study: 2-3 retrieval prompts per section, answered inline. A miss schedules that section for re-reading after 1 week, 1 month and 6 months.
5) Time-to-finish ribbon. It shows the cost of the whole book, the current chapter and the pages hot for your query at each gear, using your own measured reading rates. Example: Jevons's Principles of Science (292,116 words) takes about 19.5 h at gear 4 and about 1 h 10 m at gear 2.
6) Known-material dimmer. Tick books you've read, such as Hume's Enquiry. Paragraphs in the current book that closely restate them collapse to stubs ('restates Hume, Enquiry §X ¶12').
7) Coverage map. A strip in the style of Seesoft records how deeply you've touched each part (riffled, skimmed, read, studied), lit like the map in a Metroidvania game. In floorplan mode the strip becomes rooms sized by each chapter's word count.
- Portals mark explicit references to other books and open them at the target passage.
- A side-by-side riffle runs two books under one term heat map.
8) Sealed riffle for in-copyright books. You get the fore-edge heat, built from HTRC Extracted Features page-level token counts, plus Search Inside flags, but no text. Across books, a reliability diagram tracks how well calibrated you are about what you already know, and re-tests are scheduled as spaced retrieval.
candidates.why_clever:
Speed reading mostly doesn't work (Rayner et al. 2016), and skimming is a different task with a measurable comprehension cost. So the honest design is not a faster RSVP reader. It is a set of distinct modes, each showing its cost, with free switching that keeps your place.
- The bet supplies the decision that is usually missing. A proper scoring rule applied to your own knowledge decides which chapters get your hours.
- Because of the pretesting effect, guessing first improves retention even when the guess is wrong.
- Gears 1-2 and the digests are extractive, so you never see words the author didn't write.
- The fore-edge shows 500 pages of structure at once.
- Dog-ears turn the library into a collective annotator, using only public text.
- The coverage map turns 'have I read this book?' into a graded, visible answer across thousands of pages.
candidates.signature_moment: Six quick bets on Venn's Logic of Chance. Chapters I-V turn grey: about 0.3 bits each, so you already knew them. Chapter VIII, 'The Rule of Succession', flashes red at 3.1 bits. You put 70% on 'Venn endorses Laplace's rule as a general principle of induction', and he doesn't. Shift to gear 1 and thumb down the fore-edge until a dog-ear stands up. Stop there: 'It is hard to take such a rule as this seriously', tagged 'quoted in Dale, A History of Inverse Probability'. Press 4 and you are reading that paragraph. The verdict bar reads: 'Read 14 pages here; skim about 180 elsewhere; saved 4 h 20 min.'
screens: Shelf: full texts as spines with word count, time per gear and coverage rings
Fore-edge, edge-on: chapter bands, maths density, term heat, dog-ears
Bet card and reveal: four claims with sliders, bits scored, decisive passage highlighted
Information map: spine shaded by surprise, with recommended gears and time saved
Gear 1 riffle mid-flight with glimpse lines and speed bumps; gear 2 skim with hairlines
Gear 3 Adler card; gear 5 study prompts and re-reading schedule
Known-material dimmer on Venn ch. XVII, with the paragraphs that restate Hume collapsed
Coverage map / floorplan with portals; sealed riffle for an in-copyright book; session summary and calibration
candidates.data_needed:
Texts:
- texts/*.txt (9 now), plus about 30 public-domain texts from gutenberg.json fetched at build. Keynes is TeX/PDF only and needs conversion.

Build:
- Chapter, paragraph and sentence segmentation with stable pagination, mapping printed-TOC page numbers onto the text where the TOC gives them.
- Per-page TF-IDF vectors for speed bumps.
- Extractive sentence scores (position, definitional patterns, numbers, TextRank) and glimpse lines.
- Cross-book paragraph similarity for the dimmer.
- Dog-ears: search distinctive 10-12-word phrases with openlibrary.org/search/inside.json, deduplicating the book's own editions. Venn's sentence returns Dale's history; Laplace's 'present state of the universe' phrase returns about 625 hits.
- Bet sets for the 9 demo books: about 150 chapters × 1-3 bets, verified by a second Claude pass and spot-checked by hand.
- Adler cards and prompts for about 10 showcase books.
- HTRC Extracted Features for sealed riffles. Fetch them now: HTRC services are scheduled to be suspended at the end of December 2026.

Per-viewer state (reading rates, coverage, bets, schedule) goes in the storage or db capability, with localStorage on the wiki.
candidates.generation_role:
Deterministic: gears 1, 2 and 4, the fore-edge, dog-ears and coverage.

On the fly via sample (streaming), all labelled AI:
- Bet sets for chapters that lack one: the main claim with supporting line ranges, plus three distractors. A second call checks that each distractor is unsupported, and the page verifies the anchor quote.
- Adler cards.
- Retrieval prompts as JSON {q, a, anchor_sentence_id}.
- A jacket-flap blurb with 'who this is for / skip to'.
- 2-3 pencilled glimpse notes on a page where you pause.
For an uploaded EPUB, Claude builds the cards in the background while you riffle.

Fallback: precomputed bets, cards and prompts for the showcase books. Elsewhere, a self-rated 'could I summarise this chapter?' bet and generic self-explanation prompts.
candidates.prior_art:
- How people triage and skim: Hinze et al. 2012 (readers triaging physical books by flicking, TOC and back cover); Duggan & Payne on skimming as satisficing.
- Reading tools: Scim (arXiv 2205.04561) and the Semantic Reader Project (2303.14334); Seesoft and TileBars.
- Shared annotation: Google Books' former 'Popular passages' and Kindle Popular Highlights; fore-edge painting.
- Retention and testing: Orbit and Quantum Country's mnemonic medium; the pretesting effect (Richland, Kornell & Kao 2009); NoCha and FABLES.
- Hollow Knight-style maps.
- The anti-pattern: Spritz-style RSVP readers.
candidates.risks:
- Extractive skimming assumes modern paragraphing. Authors of the 18th and 19th centuries often put the point mid-paragraph, so show a skim-reliability note for each book.
- Distractor quality: if distractors are too easy, every chapter looks 'known', and test-taking heuristics leak the answer.
- A chapter's main claim isn't its whole value, so verdicts should say 'skip if you only need the conclusion'.
- Quotation detection is noisy: common phrases make false dog-ears, and translations are missed.
- Synthetic page numbers confuse citation.
- Time estimates are miscalibrated until the reader's rates are learned.
- It works only where you hold the text.
- Easier skimming can displace reading; the coverage map keeps that visible.
- Bet fatigue: cap at about 8 bets per book.
- Scope is large for a light prototype, so ship the bet, gears 1, 2 and 4, and coverage first.

usefulness.why: Within-book triage (which chapters to skip, skim or study, without losing your place) is a real recurring cost, and EPUB upload extends it beyond old public-domain texts to books the reader owns. The bet-and-distractor machinery is heavy and fatiguing for weekly use. Gears plus coverage would deliver most of the value.

novelty.why: Betting on each chapter's main claim, with a log score that sets the reading gear, and dog-ears drawn from later books quoting the page are new twists. Multi-speed skimming (Scim, Semantic Reader), Kindle Popular Highlights and Orbit-style prompts are prior art. It is one-book reading, not exploration across thousands.

demo.why: The fore-edge, riffle, skim and read gears are deterministic over the 9 local texts, and dog-ears via Search Inside phrase queries are feasible. A precomputed, verified bet set for one or two books takes real build time, though. There are too many gears and modes to make all of them convincing in a day, so ship the bet plus gears 1, 2 and 4.

candidates.name: Terra Incognita
candidates.tagline: Library of Congress shelf order unrolled into a world map under fog. Settle it with what you've read, forage its frontier with a stopping rule borrowed from ecology, and get a confidence interval on how much you're still missing.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) The world.
- About 6,500 works with call numbers are laid along a Gosper (flowsnake) space-filling curve in LC order and binned into about 1,200 hexes of 5-6 works each. Shelf neighbours are therefore map neighbours: QA273 (probability) borders QA276 (statistics), which borders QA279.4 (decision theory).
- LC classes are continents named from lcc-outline.json, subclasses are provinces, and outline ranges are labelled regions.
- Works with no call number wash up on an 'Uncharted Isles' archipelago. Gutenberg's 29k titles appear as hinterland density. arXiv papers are ships anchored off the nearest range.
- Terrain encodes data: elevation is edition count (classics are mountains), green settlements are free now, amber ones are borrowable, grey ruins have no ebook.
- A toggle switches from 'shelf geography' to 'semantic geography' (a UMAP embedding layout). A second embedding model flags works whose placement is unstable.
2) Settle. Paste a reading list, import an Open Library reading log, or pick a starter pack. Each work you've read reveals its hex plus a two-hex sight radius. Works you've only heard of stay half-fogged as 'rumored'.
3) Scout. Fogged hexes on your coastline are ranked by edition count x reading-log count x a free-now bonus x novelty. Click one and a Scouting Report card appears: 3-4 lines drawn only from that hex's records. For QA279.4: Raiffa's Applied Statistical Decision Theory is the capital, and Ellsberg's Risk, Ambiguity, and Decision is free today.
4) Forage a topic, e.g. 'proper scoring rules and elicitation'. Provinces become patches, and cards arrive one at a time, each built for a 10-20 second decision.
- A book card shows the signals people use at a physical shelf: cover, title, year, call number with three neighbouring spines on each side, pages, edition count, reading-log count, first sentence, access badge.
- A paper card shows title, date and the first two sentences of the abstract.
- Keys: J skip, K later, L keeper, ; start now. Digits 1-9 record P(I read at least 3 chapters within 90 days).
5) Foraging HUD. Each patch's cumulative yield is plotted against your session-average rate, the threshold in Charnov's marginal value theorem. When a patch's smoothed recent yield drops below that rate plus a travel cost, 'leave patch' fires. An in-page logistic model of your keepers then ranks the next-best patch. A wildcard patch far from your history counters the filter bubble.
6) Coverage estimator.
- Cards are drawn from independent probes: shelf neighbourhood, embedding neighbours of your keepers, keyword search, and vocabulary Claude proposes ('logarithmic score', 'incentive compatibility', 'quadratic loss').
- Capture-recapture on the overlaps between probes (Lincoln-Petersen; Chao's estimator, which is robust to some items being easier to find), plus a discovery curve, gives 'Found 34. Estimated total in this catalog: 52 (80% CI 41-77)'.
- The estimated unfound items are broken down by region, and the fog glows where they probably are.
- A stopping rule suggests quitting when the expected finds in the next 20 cards fall below your threshold.
7) Guess mode (GeoGuessr for the stacks).
- A fragment appears: an Open Library first sentence, a Gutenberg paragraph, or an arXiv abstract with names and dates redacted.
- Spread 10 chips over the fogged map and drag a year interval.
- Scoring: a log score on location, in bits against a base-rate prior, and the Gneiting-Raftery interval score on year.
- The reveal flies to the true hex, burns off its fog, and shows five neighbours on each side. A Daily 5 uses a shared seed.
8) Empire. A summary shows the share of each continent explored, territory over time, blind-spot provinces you border but have never entered, and the week's arXiv ships landing on your coasts. A 90-day resolution screen gives a Brier score and reliability diagram for your keeper forecasts, and shows which card signals actually predicted value.
candidates.why_clever:
A search box only answers questions you thought to ask. The map shows the shape of what you haven't asked about.
- Shelf order as geography inherits a century of librarians' adjacency decisions and scales it from one aisle to 7,000 works.
- It shows the reader's own field as an archipelago: forecasting is scattered across HB3730, CB158, Q375, BF441-448 and QA279, which no subject search reveals.
- Fog turns an unbounded to-read guilt list into a bounded frontier you can see.
- The foraging maths turns 'when should I stop browsing this shelf?' into a live number.
- Capture-recapture treats recall as a quantity to estimate with an interval, which a forecaster will trust more than a feeling. No search tool estimates what it missed; this one points to the region your search habits skip.
- Guess mode trains your mental map of where ideas live, using a proper scoring rule, and every reveal is a doorway into a shelf.
candidates.signature_moment: The reader pastes the 40 books they've read. The fog burns off in waves along the curve, and the camera pulls back to show a lopsided archipelago on QA273-279, BF441-448 and HB3730. They forage 'proper scoring rules' for twenty minutes in the statistics region, and the meter reads: 'About 19 relevant items likely remain (80% CI 8-40). 70% of that mass is in a region you haven't touched.' The fog over the economics continent starts to glow. They fly there and find 'Strictly Proper Mechanisms with Cooperating Players' (arXiv 1202.3710) and 'Securities Based Decision Markets' (2103.10011) moored off HB, and with each find the interval visibly tightens.
screens: World under full fog: continent outlines and LC class names only
Settle flow: paste a list, review fuzzy matches, fog burning off along the curve
Explored empire with the Access lens and glowing frontier hexes; shelf vs semantic geography toggle
Scouting Report card with read-at links (e.g. William Ascher's Forecasting, 1978, beside Superforecasting)
Forage card with neighbouring spines, signals and key hints, plus the foraging HUD and 'leave patch' prompt
Coverage estimator: probe-overlap Venn diagram, estimate with CI, discovery curve, glowing fog showing remaining items by region
Guess round: fragment card, chips on the fogged map, year interval; reveal with neighbours and bits scored
Empire summary and 90-day calibration screen
candidates.data_needed:
Sources: catalog.json (lcc, call, s, ed, rl, wtr, acc, ia, y, fs, cov); lcc-outline.json; gutenberg.json class counts; papers.json, with an arXiv-category-to-LC table.

Build-time Node script:
- Sort by LC key, place works on a Gosper curve, and bin them into hexes.
- Compute aggregates per hex: median year, access mix, top works, subjects.
- Route subject 'rivers' through the hexes they touch.
- Write templated reports. Output is a hexes.json of about 1-2 MB.

Also precomputed:
- Embeddings of title + subjects + first sentence or abstract, from two small open models; UMAP coordinates for both.
- Top-30 neighbour lists (int16 ids) and a MiniSearch index.
- A fragment pool for Guess mode, with name and date redactions and difficulty estimates.

In the page: Fuse.js for list import. Per-viewer fog, keepers, forecasts and history go in the storage capability (localStorage on the wiki).
candidates.prior_art:
- Strategy games: fog of war and lenses in Civilization and Endless Legend.
- Maps of knowledge: xkcd's 'Map of the Internet' (a Hilbert curve) as the layout precedent; Börner's Atlas of Science; Open Syllabus Galaxy; Nomic Atlas.
- Foraging: information foraging theory (Pirolli & Card 1999) and Charnov's marginal value theorem (1976).
- Estimating what's missing: capture-recapture stopping rules in systematic reviews (Kastner et al. 2009), Chao estimators, Undermind's discovery curves.
- Calibration games: GeoGuessr; CFAR's Credence Calibration Game.
- Triage: Readwise Reader and Scholar Inbox.
candidates.risks:
- LC splits ML across Q325, QA76 and TK, so adjacency sometimes separates one field. Rivers and the semantic toggle mitigate this.
- The catalog was assembled by subject queries, so the map has artificial coastlines and must say it covers 7k sampled works.
- Capture-recapture assumes independent probes and items equally easy to find. All probes favour popular items, so estimates are biased low and CIs must be widened honestly.
- Marginal-value signals are noisy below about 20 cards per patch.
- Cards built from metadata alone can be too thin.
- Guess fragments can leak the answer.
- Card fatigue sets in past about 45 minutes.
- Scope: the forage mode alone is a buildable light prototype; the full map is a deep mockup.

usefulness.why: The capture-recapture 'what am I still missing' estimate and card-based foraging are genuinely useful for literature searches a forecaster would trust. The fog map, empire and Guess mode are mostly decoration, and the estimates are biased toward popular items in a 7k sampled catalog.

novelty.why: Fog of war over LC shelf order is new. So is capture-recapture across independent search probes giving 'how much am I still missing' with a confidence interval, and so is GeoGuessr-for-the-stacks scored in bits. Undermind's discovery curves and science maps are partial precedents, and the merged concept is a grab bag that dilutes its sharpest idea.

demo.why: A fogged hex map over the 6,518 LC-classed works makes a striking screenshot, and settling or guessing on it can be real. But the Gosper-curve layout, foraging HUD, capture-recapture probes (which need embeddings) and four separate modes are far too much for a day. Guess mode alone could be a light prototype.

candidates.name: The Front Table
candidates.tagline: A bookseller's front table that re-dresses itself on any theme from the real catalog, with handwritten shelf-talkers that say which chapter to read and whether it's free tonight. Or dress it yourself by playing this week's seeded run through neighbouring shelves.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) The table, in three-quarter view:
- 12-15 books in stacks whose height follows want-to-read and reading-log counts (log-scaled);
- three books faced out as staff picks;
- an easel sign with the theme;
- handwritten shelf-talker cards tucked under the books.
Covers are prefetched Open Library thumbnails published as files, or typographic jackets styled by era.
2) Choosing a theme. Theme chips run along the table edge: 'This week', 'After Superforecasting', 'Chance before 1925 (all free)', 'The Bayesian shelf: one of each temperament', 'Arguments against your priors', 'Under 200 pages'. Or type any theme, and a two-slip reference interview asks your purpose (a decision this week, or background) and your time budget.
3) Claude assembles the table with page tools: search_catalog, shelf_neighbors, get_work, access_status, search_papers, remainder_candidates. The page enforces hard constraints:
- every item is a real catalog, Gutenberg or arXiv id;
- at least three are readable free tonight;
- the table includes one public-domain classic, one current arXiv 'pamphlet', one dissent, and one surprise from a distant LC class.
4) Books slide on one at a time while their talkers write themselves, for example 'Read ch. VIII and skip the rest. Free: Gutenberg #57359' or 'Pairs with arXiv 2603.05544'. Each factual claim carries a tiny provenance mark (call number, OL id), and quotes are string-matched against the embedded text.
5) Pick up a book and its card flips to the pitch: why it's here, what it argues against, who should not buy it, and access-router chips.
6) A re-dress dial moves the table between classic and current, short and deep, and 'free only'.
7) The remainder bin is a crate under the table holding durable but neglected books, ranked by editions ÷ want-to-read. Examples: Bolstad's Introduction to Bayesian Statistics (11 editions, 1 want-to-read), Parnell's Handbook of Decision Analysis, Fenton & Neil's Risk Assessment and Decision Analysis with Bayesian Networks, Pohl's Cognitive Illusions.
8) The Delve: dress the table yourself.
- Each Sunday a seed generates a branching map of 7 floors in the style of Slay the Spire.
- Each node type moves you a different way: Shelf Step (a few call numbers away); Subject Portal (a jump through a shared LC subject heading); Time Rift (same subject, at least 80 years older, landing in the public domain); Wildcard (an arXiv paper sharing a theme); Elite (a textbook over 600 pages); Rest (a short free essay); Merchant (the access router).
- At each node you draft 1 of 3 cards, and your pick anchors the next floor.
- Relics are the table's constraints made playable: 'Lantern of Gutenberg' (all picks free today), 'Pre-1950', 'Obscurity', 'Three continents'.
- The finished 5-7 card deck becomes your table, with a story of the run. Seeds can be shared.
9) A window-display archive keeps past tables and runs.
candidates.why_clever:
- A front table compresses thousands of books into a 12-item argument you can accept or reject in 30 seconds.
- Recommenders return 'more like this'. A table states a thesis and builds in contrast: the dissent, the old book, the far-class surprise.
- Generation is constrained by tools and every id is validated, so the books are always real and routable.
- The remainder metric (editions ÷ readers) finds books that kept being reprinted while nobody talks about them, which popularity rankings never surface.
- The Delve gives serendipity a structure. It limits randomness to the three adjacencies a reader already trusts (shelf, subject, time) and forces a choice at each step: about 21 works considered and 6 chosen. That makes a weekly ritual and something to share.
candidates.signature_moment: Type 'Before you trust a forecast' and the table is swept clear. Laplace's A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities lands first, faced out, with a card: '"it is a bet of 1826214 to one that it will rise again to-morrow". The original overconfident forecast. Free tonight.' Venn's The Logic of Chance lands beside it: 'Venn's reply: "It is hard to take such a rule as this seriously."' Then come Superforecasting (stacked high), Kahneman, Sibony & Sunstein's Noise, and Perrow's Normal Accidents as the far-class surprise. Last is a thin arXiv pamphlet, 'Prediction Markets Underperform Simple Baselines For Infectious Disease Forecasting' (2605.11220): 'The dissent. Read the abstract before you read Tetlock.'
