Reference-interview slips (purpose, time budget)
Re-dressing: books sliding in, talkers streaming in a handwritten face
Book picked up: pitch card with provenance marks and access chips
Re-dress dial and remainder-bin crate with editions-to-readers ratios
Delve map: branching floors, node icons, path so far, relic draft
Delve encounter: draft 1 of 3 with 'why here' lines; Time Rift transition
End-of-run deck dealt onto the table; window-display archive; validation inspector showing rejected ids
candidates.data_needed:
Sources: catalog.json (wtr, rl, ed, acc, pp, y, call, lcc, fs, cov, s, pg/se/lv), gutenberg.json, papers.json, openstax.json.

Precompute:
- Remainder candidates: ed ≥ 8 and low wtr, filtered to the reader's domains.
- Call-number neighbour lists.
- A subject-to-works inverted index, for Subject Portals.
- A quality filter removing solutions manuals, duplicate works, fiction and foreign-language noise.
- A seeded PRNG for runs.
- About 20 tables generated by Claude and checked by hand, for the fallback and the weekly rotation.
- Verified quotations from the Gutenberg texts for talkers.
- Cover thumbnails for about 600 likely books, published as files, since the artifact can't fetch covers.openlibrary.org.
candidates.prior_art:
- Bookselling and libraries: independent bookstores' front tables and shelf-talkers; library displays and LibGuides pathfinders; the RUSA reference interview; 'blind date with a book' displays; StackLife.
- Curation and recommendation: Five Books; LibraryThing's Unsuggester; Open Syllabus co-assignment.
- Games and serendipity: Slay the Spire's branching map and card draft; Wordle and Spelunky daily seeds; The Wiki Game; StumbleUpon.
candidates.risks:
- Generated cards can sound authoritative while being wrong about a book's content. Limit factual claims to metadata and verified quotes, and phrase judgements as the bookseller's opinion.
- Catalog noise (fiction, self-help, foreign editions) needs filtering.
- Covers raise size and rights questions.
- Want-to-read counts skew toward pop titles, so log-scale the stacks.
- Gutenberg's y field is the year a book was added, so Time Rifts need real dates.
- The Delve's novelty fades unless the deck is genuinely good. Judge it by the reading slate it produces.

usefulness.why: A weekly, contrast-built table with chapter-level 'read this, it's free tonight' talkers and the editions-to-readers remainder bin is a decent serendipity feed. It is push discovery, though, not help with a reader's own pressing questions, generated talkers can misstate content, and the Delve game adds little usefulness.

novelty.why: LLM-curated themed lists are what every chatbot already produces, and shelf-talkers are a skin on that. The genuinely fresh parts are the 'remainder bin' metric (editions ÷ want-to-read) and the Delve, a Slay-the-Spire run across shelf, subject and time adjacencies.

demo.why: A table of real covers (6,601 works have cov ids for build-time thumbnails) with handwritten talkers makes a very legible, attractive first screen. The quotes in the signature moment are verified. About 20 validated precomputed tables plus a live tool-constrained assembly fill the day; the Delve is a second app and should be cut.

candidates.name: The Bindery
candidates.tagline: Describe the book you wish existed, or draw a line across the map of knowledge, and get a bound volume of real chapters, papers and lecture segments, with an editor's notes between them and a spine that thickens or thins with the hours you have.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Two ways in.
- A brief: topic, level, purpose and hours, e.g. 'Judging forecasts, from Laplace to proper scoring rules; technical; 8 hours'.
- A gesture: on the shared embedding map of ~37k items (from Sieve's build), draw a stroke from one region to another, say Classical probability to Bayesian statistics to AI alignment. The stroke is sampled into about 10 stops.
2) A corridor search at each stop returns about 15 candidate units: whole books, chapters (from Open Library TOCs, parsed Gutenberg chapter headings and OpenStax sections), arXiv papers, and lecture segments (from Synteny's boards).
3) Claude acts as series editor, with page tools candidates_near(stop), search_catalog, get_toc, search_fulltext, search_papers and access_route. It:
- picks 1-3 tracks per chapter, so each step is small;
- prefers free or borrowable units when quality is close;
- sets page ranges;
- gives each track a depth (gist / skim / read / study) and a value score;
- writes a 100-150 word editor's bridge before each chapter: why this comes next, and what to look for.
A resolver gate drops any track that doesn't resolve to a record id and lists it as 'could not verify'.
4) Binding. An animated book appears with a generated title and a gold-stamped spine. The TOC shows access chips, page ranges and minutes for each track. The colophon gives total pages, estimated hours, access mix ('6 free, 3 borrowable, 1 buy') and cost.
5) Hours slider (1-40 h). A deterministic knapsack in the page reallocates depth by value per minute, with no model call. At 2 h most tracks become one-paragraph gists and two are read in full; at 20 h whole chapters and exercises come in. The spine visibly thickens or thins.
6) 'Free only' swaps paid tracks for the nearest open equivalent and shows what each swap loses.
7) Riffle the volume. Free chapters are readable inline between the bridges (Gutenberg text, arXiv abstract, OpenStax section). Others show their card and access route.
8) Shelve and schedule.
- Claude assigns a plausible LC call number, and the volume appears as a 'phantom' spine among real neighbours in the stacks.
- Export a weekly schedule with spaced revisits (Markdown, ICS), or send the volume to the Reading Portfolio.
- A shelf of 'books that don't exist' holds precomputed volumes: 'Scoring Rules for Forecasters', 'The Bayesian Revival', 'From Cybernetics to Alignment', 'Information Theory for Forecasters'.
candidates.why_clever:
Researchers don't lack reading lists; they lack sequences with depths and time costs.
- The Bindery turns curriculum design into drawing a line or writing a one-line brief.
- It works by transclusion (Ted Nelson's term) rather than generated text: you read the real Laplace, the real Venn and the real arXiv paper, and Claude writes only the joins.
- Choosing at chapter level breaks the whole-book unit that makes reading across disciplines expensive.
- The hours slider turns Adler's levels of reading into an explicit allocation problem, close to value of information per minute.
- The colophon puts the true cost of a self-made syllabus on the cover.
- Every track must resolve to a record id, so the model cannot invent a source.
candidates.signature_moment: You draw a lazy S-curve from the bottom-left island (Laplace, Hume, Venn) to the AI-alignment peninsula. Ten stops light up along it, an editor's note types itself between them, and a gold-stamped spine slides onto the shelf: 'From Chance to Corrigibility'. Chapter 1 is Laplace's actual 'Concerning Illusions in the Estimation of Probabilities' from Gutenberg #58881, readable right there. The colophon reads '312 pp, about 11 h, 6 free tonight, 3 borrowable, 1 library hold'. You drag the hours slider from 11 to 2, and the spine visibly thins as chapters fold into one-paragraph gists.
screens: Map with drawing tool, plus a brief composer with example briefs and hours slider
Path sampled into stops, with corridor candidates fanned out at each
Editor at work: picks locking in stop by stop, tool-call log, bridges streaming
Bound volume: cover, spine, TOC with tracks, depths, minutes and access chips
Colophon and access summary with 'free only' substitutions and what each loses
Budget states: the same volume at 2 h, 8 h and 20 h
Inline riffle of a free chapter between two bridges
Phantom volume shelved among real neighbours; shelf of saved volumes; schedule export
candidates.data_needed:
Sources:
- The shared embedding map and kNN index, from Sieve's build.
- catalog.json: acc, ia, pp, call, s, ed.
- gutenberg.json and texts: passage ids and chapter boundaries for about 300 public-domain books in the reader's classes.
- papers.json, and section URLs from openstax.json.
- Open Library TOCs for about 500 key works, fetched at build.
- Lecture segments, if Synteny is built.

Precompute:
- Minutes per track at each depth: pages × words per page ÷ a reading rate for that depth.
- Corridor candidate lists for 5 demo paths.
- 5 complete volumes with bridges.
candidates.generation_role:
Live and central: Claude picks a unit for each stop using the tools, assigns value scores and depths, writes the editor's bridges (≤150 words, labelled AI), chooses the title and call number, and turns a brief into waypoints on the map.

Deterministic in the page: the allocator, access routing, cost totals and schedule, so the slider responds instantly.

Fallback: the 5 precomputed volumes. A drawn path or brief still produces an algorithmic volume, labelled as such and without bridges: the nearest well-rated accessible unit at each stop, deduplicated and ordered by LCC, then decade.
candidates.prior_art:
- Vannevar Bush's memex trails (1945); Ted Nelson's transclusion and Xanadu.
- Assembled readers: university coursepacks; Pressbooks and remixed open educational resources; Wikipedia Books (PediaPress).
- Curricula: Open Syllabus; Metacademy roadmaps.
- Generated study material: NotebookLM and Google's Learn Your Way; AutoSurvey (arXiv 2406.10252) and InteractiveSurvey (2504.08762).
- Generated playlists; Bret Victor-style direct manipulation.
candidates.risks:
- Sparse TOCs for in-copyright books make chapter picks guesses ('whole book, chapter suggested from title only').
- Page ranges are unknown for most in-copyright books.
- Bridges may overstate what unread chapters contain. Ground them in TOC and abstract text, and label them.
- Paths through empty map regions produce awkward jumps. Show 'gap' markers rather than hiding them.
- Time and value estimates are rough.
- 'Free only' substitutions may teach worse, which is why each swap shows what it loses.
- A generated syllabus may be trusted more than it deserves; the tool log and the 'could not verify' list push back.

usefulness.why: A sequenced, chapter-level, access-aware syllabus with an hours slider squarely serves 'understand a new field within my time budget', with less hallucination risk than asking a chatbot. The weak points are sparse in-copyright tables of contents and page ranges, and a draw-a-line gesture that is more novelty than tool. Brief-to-volume plus the slider is the useful core.

novelty.why: Drawing a stroke across the knowledge map to get a transcluded volume, whose spine thickens or thins with your hours, is a fresh gesture. But generated syllabi and courses are now commonplace (NotebookLM, Learn Your Way, any chatbot), so what is new is the gesture plus the knapsack, not the concept.

demo.why: It depends on Sieve's embedding map and on chapter-level units, but catalog.json has zero TOCs, so in-copyright tracks become whole-book guesses. The bound-volume animation and the hours slider are demo-able only over a few hand-built volumes.

candidates.name: Core Sample
candidates.tagline: Point at any 2026 preprint, or name a goal, and Claude drills down through the prerequisites, from recent papers through textbooks to 18th-century bedrock. The page then finds the cheapest route back up from what you already know.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Input. Pick a recent paper from papers.json, paste any abstract, or type a goal: 'design a proper scoring rule for free-text LLM forecasts', 'be ready for Gelman's Bayesian Data Analysis ch. 5', 'understand Pearl's do-calculus'. Mark the works you've read, by import or by ticking; they turn gold.
2) Drill. Claude runs a tool loop (search_papers, search_catalog, search_gutenberg, search_passages, get_item, get_toc, reading_cost). It streams 4-8 load-bearing concepts plus prerequisite links, each with a one-line 'needed because'.
- Claude may name a node only by an id that exists in the data.
- Anything else is drawn as a dashed 'uncharted' node with a 'search outside' link, never as a real card.
- A ticker shows the tool calls as they happen.
3) Core view. Concepts run along the x-axis and log time down the y-axis, from 2026 at the top to 1748 at the bottom.
- Layers are coloured by genre: preprint, textbook, popular synthesis, classic.
- Each concept's drill hole descends through the layers to the deepest item in the corpus, marked 'bedrock in this corpus', not 'origin'.
- Each layer card shows a one-line 'what this layer adds' (labelled AI), an access badge, minutes, and for classics a passage link.
4) Tree view. The same graph as a tech tree in the style of Civilization: the goal at the right edge, columns by prerequisite depth.
- Node cards show hours, access and year.
- Gold nodes you've already read grant 'Eureka' boosts that halve the cost of nodes built on them.
5) Route solver. Given your access keys (shared with the Circulation Desk) and a time budget, it finds the cheapest route up: 'Free route: 31 h, $0, 6 of 9 free' against 'Fast route: 19 h, one purchase'.
- Rigorous and practitioner branches are shown side by side.
- Any node offers 'why this node?' and 'reroll branch'.
6) Seams. Where several drill holes share a layer, a horizontal seam lights up. It shows how few roots the newest work rests on.
7) Blueprint view (headset or delight mode). The graph is extruded as a miniature building on your desk:
- rooms are concepts, sized by how much literature the catalog holds;
- doors are prerequisites;
- plinths hold canonical works;
- the basement holds public-domain history;
- the light level is the fraction readable free.
Pinch the entrance to shrink inside and walk the route.
8) Export the route to the Bindery (as a volume), the Reading Portfolio (as a queue) or Gearbox (as a reading list with depths). Rooms and nodes you've read stay lit, so the core doubles as a coverage map.
candidates.why_clever:
Citation-graph tools show neighbouring papers and stop there. But concepts are actually taught in textbooks and old books.
- Core Sample builds a stack of prerequisites that crosses genres, with time as depth, so you can see how old the idea under you is.
- The route up answers a planning question search can't: what is the least I must read to understand this paper, given what I already know, and at what cost?
- Costs and existing knowledge make the plan personal and let routes be compared.
- It turns 1,457 arXiv papers into 1,457 entry points into a 37,000-work library.
- The id-only rule plus client-side validation keeps every node real and reachable, not a plausible syllabus of books that may not exist.
candidates.signature_moment: Press Drill on 'Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles' (arXiv 2607.18269, May 2026). The core descends past the AIA Forecaster technical report (2025), Tetlock's Superforecasting (2015) and Surowiecki's The Wisdom of Crowds (2004). Then it hits bedrock 212 years down, at Laplace's 1814 chapter 'Concerning the Probability of the Judgments of Tribunals', where he applies crowd arithmetic to judges. A seam lights up to show the same chapter under the 'independence of errors' hole too. Two layers are already gold from your reading log, and the footer reads 'route up: about 9 h, 6 of 8 free'.
screens: Paper or goal picker with themes, recency, 'paste an abstract' and already-read chips
Drilling (streaming): concepts extracted, holes descending, tool-call ticker
Core diagram: concept holes x log-time layers, genre colours, bedrock markers, seams
Layer card: what it adds, passage link, access, minutes, Eureka boost
Tech-tree view with the free route highlighted and a cost footer; two routes compared
Blueprint miniature on a desk with a lifted room and door-rationale card; walk-in interior
Export: route to Bindery, Portfolio or Gearbox; static fallback banner
candidates.data_needed:
Sources:
- papers.json (abstracts, themes, dates); catalog.json (y, lcc, s, acc, pp); openstax.json (84 CC BY textbooks, e.g. Introductory Statistics 2e); lcc-outline.json.
- gutenberg.json and texts, for passage ids. Gutenberg's y field is the year added, so classics are dated from author and title metadata or Wikidata.

Build time:
- Open Library TOCs, for nodes at chapter level.
- Crossref reference lists for works with DOIs, to seed real prerequisite links.
- A BM25/MiniSearch index over titles, subjects, abstracts and passages.
- About 12 fully drilled cores (two per paper theme) and 6 goal trees, saved as JSON. Goals: scoring rules, hierarchical Bayes, causal inference, judgmental forecasting, information theory, AI alignment foundations.
- A small procedural-architecture kit in three.js for the Blueprint view.
candidates.generation_role:
Generated on the fly: concept extraction; choosing layers and nodes through tools; the 'needed because' and 'what this adds' lines; 'why this node'; and 'reroll branch'.

Client side: id validation, layout (dagre/ELK), cost maths, seams and the route solver.

Fallback:
- The precomputed cores and trees.
- For any other paper, a keyword-only drill: abstract terms are matched against subjects and passages with BM25, and hits are grouped by era, with no generated labels.
- A deterministic 'tree from subjects' mode, which approximates prerequisites as older, more general works in the same LC range.
candidates.prior_art:
- Concept maps: Metacademy (Grosse & Reed) concept graphs; Khan Academy's knowledge map; roadmap.sh; Civilization tech trees.
- Citation tools: Connected Papers' 'prior works'; Litmaps; CiteSee; Choe et al. 2024, 'Fields, Bridges, and Foundations' (arXiv 2405.07267); 'Leveraging Citation Networks to Visualize Scholarly Influence Over Time' (1611.07135).
- Spatial metaphors: stratigraphic columns; World-in-Miniature (Stoakley, Conway & Pausch, CHI 1995); the method of loci.
candidates.risks:
- The model can invent a plausible but unhistorical lineage. Label links 'conceptual ancestor in this corpus', never 'cited by'.
- The corpus lacks many true primary sources (Brier 1950, de Finetti, Savage, Gneiting & Raftery), so bedrock is relative to the corpus and must say so.
- Prerequisite orderings are judgement calls.
- Most works lack TOCs, so nodes are often whole books.
- The paper set leans toward ML.
- Tool loops cost many calls, so cap and cache them.
- The architectural metaphor imposes a hierarchy, so keep the 2D views primary.

usefulness.why: 'What is the least I must read, given what I know, to understand this paper' is a real planning question, and the route solver with already-read nodes addresses it. The drill to 18th-century bedrock is more charming than useful, prerequisite links are LLM judgement calls, and it overlaps heavily with the Bindery.

novelty.why: Drilling from a 2026 preprint down through textbooks to 1814 'bedrock', with time as depth and genre as strata, is a striking picture across genres. Connected Papers' prior works and Metacademy stop at papers or at a flat graph. The tech-tree and route-solver views are more familiar, and the blueprint view is decoration.

demo.why: The precomputed cores and a stratigraphic SVG are buildable, and the Laplace 'Judgments of Tribunals' chapter exists, so the bedrock moment works. But the lineages are model-invented, the corpus lacks most true primary sources, and making 12 trustworthy cores, a tech tree and a blueprint view in a day is unrealistic.

candidates.name: Crux Table
candidates.tagline: Adler's Syntopicon rebuilt for each question. TileBars show where every book on the shelf discusses it, Claude maps the authors' vocabularies onto shared terms, and a matrix ties each author's stance on each sub-question to a verified sentence. Any two authors can be collapsed to the one row they really disagree on.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Pick or type a contested question. Presets:
- 'Is the principle of indifference sound?'
- 'Can past regularity justify near-certainty that the sun will rise tomorrow?'
- 'Can testimony ever make a miracle credible?'
- 'Is probability in the mind or in the world?'
- 'Is it wrong to believe on insufficient evidence?'
- A modern set: 'Can expert forecasters be trusted?'
2) The shelf: about 16-20 public-domain works in full text, in date order.
- The 9 in texts/: Hume, Laplace, Jevons, Venn, Russell, Poincaré, Peirce, Mill, Darwin.
- Fetched at build time: Keynes's Treatise #32625, Boole's Laws of Thought #15114, Mill's System of Logic #27942, De Morgan's Budget of Paradoxes #23100, Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' #50189, James's The Will to Believe #26659, Poincaré's Science and Hypothesis #37157, Bacon's Novum Organum #45988.
- In-copyright works sit as ghost columns with page pointers only: Jaynes, Kadane's Rethinking the Foundations of Statistics, McGrayne. For the modern set: Tetlock, Taleb, Silver and Noise, plus arXiv 2511.07678, 2607.18269 and 2605.11220, quoted only by verified abstract span.
3) FIND. A TileBars overview draws each book as a bar of about 120 segments, shaded by in-browser BM25 relevance, with chapter ticks. You see in one glance where everyone discusses the question, before any generation. A harvest view shows Claude's search_passages, read_passage and neighbors calls as they run.
4) SHARED TERMS (Rosetta grid). Claude proposes 4-8 neutral terms, e.g. 'prior improbability of the reported event', 'reliability of the witness', 'independence of witnesses'. Each cell holds that author's own word in bold and a verbatim span, which the page renders from a passage id. A toggle re-renders every quote in the shared terms.
5) CRUX MATRIX. Rows are 4-6 sub-questions; columns are the works, in date order. Each cell holds:
- a stance glyph: affirms / denies / conditional / silent;
- an evidence-type badge: formal derivation, thought experiment, appeal to authority, empirical tally;
- a short quote. Claude proposes line ranges; the page extracts and checks the text, then shows 'matches line N' or drops the cell.
Red brackets connect cells that contradict each other.
6) CRUX DIFF. Select any two works and the table collapses to the rows where they diverge, sorted by how much of the disagreement each explains. Each row is labelled fact, definition (a verbal dispute) or value.
7) ANALYZE. For quantitative sub-questions, a formalisation panel proposes a shared model (posterior odds = prior odds × the likelihood ratio of the testimony) with sliders. Each author's stated verdict is drawn as the region they would accept. A 'what would change their mind' column lists the evidence each side admits as relevant.
8) Verify. A minimum reading set (about 12 passages, with minutes and links) is enough to check every cell. Clicking a cell opens the reader at that paragraph, with the book's TileBar as its scrollbar. Reject a cell to re-run it, or export the table as a wiki note with citations.
candidates.why_clever:
Search and lists return documents. The reader's real question is where the disagreement lives.
- The table compresses many books into the few sub-claims that do the work.
- It separates verbal disputes from substantive ones, which most syntopical reading and most AI summaries blur.
- Adler's steps 2-4 (a neutral vocabulary, neutral questions, defining the issues) are what LLMs do unusually well and humans find hardest. Step 1 and all the evidence stay verbatim and checkable, and the TileBars work with no model at all.
- Every cell carries a quote checked against the text, so the result is an index you can audit, not an essay. 'Which book should I read to settle this?' becomes answerable.
- Britannica's 1952 Syntopicon took years to cover 102 ideas. This builds one for any question in about a minute.
candidates.signature_moment: The reader selects Laplace and Venn, and six rows collapse to one glowing sub-question: 'Is the uniform prior a fact about our ignorance, or a claim about the world?' On the left, Laplace (line 610): '...it is a bet of 1826214 to one that it will rise again to-morrow.' On the right, Venn, ch. VIII, explains that he traces the Rule's origin '...to show what astonishing conclusions are apt to be accepted on the supposed warrant of mathematics.' Both carry green 'verified, line N' badges. The verbal-dispute detector notes that they use 'probability' in different senses. The glossary toggle rewrites both quotes in shared terms, and the disagreement visibly shrinks to one row.
screens: Debate lobby: question cards with seated works as spines (year, access badge)
TileBars overview: whole-book relevance strips per work with hover snippets; harvest view with tool log
Rosetta grid: neutral terms x authors, each cell showing the author's term and a verified span
Crux matrix streaming: stances, evidence badges, verification flipping grey to green or red, rejected cells struck through
Crux Diff of two works with fact / definition / value labels
Formalisation panel: shared likelihood-ratio model with author verdict regions
Cell drawer / reader with the TileBar scrollbar and context
Minimum reading set and export; offline banner with precomputed tables
candidates.data_needed:
Full texts:
- Gutenberg texts for about 16-30 works (the 9 local ones plus fetches at build time).
- Split into paragraphs with chapter and line locators.
- Gzip-stored or lazy-loaded per book (about 6-9 MB).
- An in-browser BM25 index (MiniSearch) over about 30,000 passage ids.

Other data:
- catalog.json for ghost columns; papers.json abstracts for the modern debate.
- Page-level hit lists for ghost works from Internet Archive / Open Library Search Inside, for about 50 terms.

Precomputed: complete, spot-checked tables for about 6 questions, including sunrise/induction; credibility of testimony (Hume's 'Of Miracles', Laplace on testimonies, Venn ch. XVII); principle of indifference; and expert forecasting.
candidates.prior_art:
- Adler & Van Doren, How to Read a Book (syntopical reading), and the Great Books Syntopicon (1952).
- Hearst's TileBars (CHI 1995).
- Argument mapping: Kialo, Argdown, Rationale, and Horn's 'Can Computers Think?' debate maps.
- CFAR's Double Crux.
- AI research tools: Elicit's papers-by-questions table, Consensus and scite, STORM/Co-STORM.
- Anthropic's Citations API pattern.
candidates.risks:
- Stances can be misattributed in 18th- and 19th-century prose (irony, views stated only to be rejected). Verification blocks fabricated quotes, not out-of-context ones, so context stays one click away.
- 'Inferential linking' errors map two authors onto one term when they mean different things.
- Sub-questions can be over-constructed, issue maps can impose false binaries, and seating fringe works beside consensus ones creates false balance.
- Retrieval misses period vocabulary.
- In-copyright works get only page pointers or short quotes.
- A live 8-work table takes about 20-40 tool calls and 30-90 s, so it must stream and cache.

usefulness.why: Locating where authors disagree is valuable when comparing treatments, and verified quotes make it auditable. But the full-text corpus is 19th-century philosophy of probability, and modern works get only page pointers or abstract spans, so the reader would use it for occasional deep dives, not to decide what to read.

novelty.why: A Syntopicon built per question over centuries of full texts, with verified quotes in the stance cells. 'Crux diff' collapses two authors to the one row they really disagree on, and verbal disputes are flagged. That goes well past Elicit's paper×question tables and Kialo, but it shares much of its mechanism with Great Conversation.

demo.why: The TileBars are instant and easy, and the Laplace/Venn quotes are verified. But a credible stance matrix across 16-20 old books needs careful hand-checking of attributions, because a wrong stance sinks the demo. A live run takes 30-90 s, and the concept overlaps heavily with the Great Conversation.

candidates.name: Chapter Lenses
candidates.tagline: Each chapter gets the interface its content calls for: live arithmetic, an argument tree, a cast list. Claude builds it from a typed kit in which every element points back to the text.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Open any chapter of a local full text. It reads as plain text, with a rail of lenses beside it.
2) Claude reads the chapter in chunks through a read(book, from, to) tool and picks 1-3 lenses from a fixed, typed component kit:
- WorkedNumbers: each numerical claim, with a formula in a tiny safe expression language that the page recomputes live.
- ArgumentTree: claims, supports and objections.
- ClaimLedger: each claim with its examples.
- Timeline.
- DramatisPersonae: the people cited, with where and why.
- PeriodGlossary: old terms mapped to modern ones.
- SelfTest questions.
3) The output is a JSON spec, validated against the kit's schema. Every leaf carries line pointers plus an anchor string, which the page verifies. Nodes that fail verification render hatched.
4) Lenses and text are linked both ways. Hovering a node highlights its lines; selecting lines shows which nodes cite them.
5) Lenses can be edited in plain language: 'only Mill's own claims, not the objections he states', or 'add a timeline of the people he cites'. Claude edits the spec, and the page shows a diff of it.
6) Cached lenses are published as JSON so the static wiki can show them. PeriodGlossary entries accumulate across books into a running translation layer for old texts.
7) Any node offers 'read in context', which opens Gearbox at that passage.
candidates.why_clever:
Every reading app gives every book the same interface. Here the model decides what form a chapter needs: a probability argument wants live numbers, an essay wants an argument tree, natural history wants claims with their examples.
- The model can only compose verified components from a small kit, so the generated UI stays checkable instead of turning into a fluent paraphrase.
- Readers get fast structural access to dense 19th-century prose without the prose being replaced.
- Computed lenses can catch errors no summary would, because the page does the arithmetic, not the model.
candidates.signature_moment: The reader opens Laplace's Philosophical Essay on Probabilities at 'Concerning the Probabilities of Testimonies'. The WorkedNumbers lens extracts his urn of 1,000 numbers and his witness who deceives one time in ten, recomputes each step, and one step turns red. The text multiplies 1/1000 by 'the probability 6/10 of the veracity of the witness' and gets 9/10000, but 1/1000 × 6/10 = 6/10000. The lens shows that 9/10 makes the arithmetic work. It links the file's own transcriber's note, which promises '9/10 in place of 6/10, on page 110', a correction this copy never received. A slider on the witness's reliability then lets the reader watch Laplace's posterior move. Switching to Mill's On Liberty, ch. II, the same rail becomes an argument tree of his grounds for freedom of opinion.
screens: Library: books and chapters, with badges marking cached lenses
Reader: plain text with the lens rail collapsed
WorkedNumbers (Laplace on testimonies): steps recomputed, the mismatch in red, a reliability slider
ArgumentTree (Mill ch. II): claims, supports and objections linked to lines
DramatisPersonae and PeriodGlossary (Jevons, Venn): people cited; old terms mapped to modern
Lens editing: a plain-language request, the spec diff, before and after
Verification overlay: hatched unverified nodes and the raw spec
candidates.data_needed:
- texts/*.txt, split into chapters at build time. A regex on CHAPTER/SECTION headings does the split, checked by hand for the 9 books, with [Pg N] maps.
- A component kit in vanilla JS or React UMD, with its JSON schema.
- A small safe arithmetic evaluator (fractions, products, powers).
- Precomputed lens specs for about 12 showcase chapters: Laplace on testimonies; Hume's 'Of Miracles'; Venn ch. VIII (Rule of Succession) and ch. XVII (Credibility of Extraordinary Stories); Mill ch. II; Darwin ch. IV; Russell ch. VI; Jevons on the Logical Machine; Peirce's 'The Doctrine of Chances'.
candidates.prior_art:
- Reading aids: Allen AI's Semantic Reader (ScholarPhi definitions, Scim skimming highlights, CiteSee); LiquidText.
- Generative interfaces: Google's generative UI in Gemini ('dynamic view', 2025); Anthropic's Imagine with Claude (2025); Ink & Switch's essay on malleable software (2025).
- Explorable explanations: Bret Victor (2011).
- Argument mapping: Rationale and Kialo.
candidates.risks:
- Gimmick risk: many chapters just want to be read, so plain text stays the default.
- A lens is an interpretation and can impose structure the author did not intend. Label it as such and keep the source one click away.
- Reading a 10,000-word chapter costs time and tokens, so caching matters.
- Formula extraction can be wrong, so show both the author's number and the recomputed one, and never silently 'fix' the text.
- A spec can pass the schema and still be shallow.

usefulness.why: It is a clever generative-UI demo (the Laplace arithmetic catch is memorable), but per-chapter bespoke interfaces on a handful of public-domain texts won't be part of a weekly reading workflow, and its own risks section concedes most chapters just want to be read.

novelty.why: Generative UI per piece of content is already a product category (Gemini dynamic view, Imagine with Claude). The typed, pointer-verified kit and live recomputation are a real twist, and catching an actual erratum in Laplace is a memorable demo.

demo.why: The signature moment is real. I verified that Laplace's text multiplies 1/1000 by '6/10' to get 9/10000, at line 2890, and that the file's own transcriber's note promises a correction this copy never received. That is a 30-second demo no summary tool can match. With 3 kit components, about 5 precomputed specs over local texts and deterministic pointer checks, it is functional in a day, though the resting screenshot is just text plus a side rail.

candidates.name: Reading Portfolio
candidates.tagline: Each Monday your open questions, hours and access become a reading plan at chapter level, ranked by how far each item is expected to move your credence per hour. Each Sunday the desk scores your forecasts about your own reading.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Setup, once.
- Write 3-8 live, resolvable questions with current credences, Fatebook-style. Examples: 'P(an AI system matches the superforecaster median on ForecastBench before 2028)'; 'P(prediction markets beat simple statistical baselines for epidemic forecasting)'; 'How should LLM forecasters be scored on long-horizon questions?'
- Set a weekly budget, say 6 hours and $20.
- Set the access keys you hold (shared with the Circulation Desk).
2) Inbox. Items arrive from three sources: new arXiv papers in your themes since last Monday (papers.json has about 8-14 a week in 2026), items sent from other tools, and pasted bibliographies parsed into catalog matches.
3) Triage strip. J/K moves, Y/N/L decides. Each card carries an Evidence Pre-read:
- relevance to each question and expected direction;
- a 10/50/90 credence shift in log-odds;
- the crux it bears on;
- an evidence grade (benchmark result, RCT, theory, survey, anecdote);
- the abstract sentence the pre-read relies on;
- an hours estimate (pages times a per-genre minutes-per-page prior);
- an access chip.
4) Frontier. Every candidate is a dot: hours on a log x-axis, expected |shift| on y, with whiskers.
- Books with TOCs split into chapter dots, so a whole book and its best chapters compete separately.
- The Pareto frontier is drawn, and the budget is a vertical line.
- A risk slider runs from 'maximise mean' to 'maximise 10th percentile', and a knapsack picks the week.
- Dragging your prior on a question re-scores everything live, because an item's value depends on where you stand.
5) The desk. Picks land on an inclined desk in the style of Data Mountain, with three depth bands: front = this week (default 70%), middle = this month (30%), back ridge = someday (5%).
- Placement is a forecast that you'll read the item; twist a card to adjust it.
- Left-right placement is yours, for example piles by landmark ('scoring rules by the lamp').
- Cards never move on their own. Untouched cards gather dust, and about 60 card spaces force decisions.
- On Quest or Android XR, WebXR hit-test anchors the desk to your real desk in passthrough. The flat desk is the default.
6) Reading log. Before opening an item you log P(this moves me by more than 5 points). Afterwards you log your new credence and a one-line note. The question's credence sparkline is annotated with the item that moved it.
7) Sunday sweep. A desk lamp passes over the front band: read cards glow and unread ones go grey. The blotter then shows:
- a reliability diagram for your placement forecasts and your 'will it move me' forecasts;
- the recommender's calibration (Claude's predicted shift against the realised shift);
- which signals actually predicted updates (recency, venue, author, Claude's pre-read);
- stale questions.
'Blow the dust' gives 3-line, abstract-only gists so you can archive cards without guilt.
8) Monday card. The week's plan, with deep links to the right page (archive.org/details/{ia}/page/n{N} for a borrowable chapter), calendar blocks, carry-over, and a footer such as 'This week: 5h40m, $0, 4 tabs'.
candidates.why_clever:
A reading list is a decision under uncertainty, but every tool ranks by topical similarity or popularity. This one ranks by the expected information an item gives about questions the reader actually holds, net of hours and access cost.
- It drops the whole book as the default unit, so chapters and papers compete on one axis.
- It shows hundreds of candidates and why each one lost, with uncertainty, rather than a ranked list.
- It closes the loop with proper scoring of both the reader and the recommender. After a few months it can say from the data whether 'Claude thinks this will move you' or 'recent preprint' predicts real updates.
- The desk uses the best-evidenced spatial effect (Data Mountain), respects the finding that free depth hurts, and makes the opportunity cost of a queue physical.
This is the concept the reader would open every week.
candidates.signature_moment: The reader drags their credence on 'AI beats superforecasters before 2028' from 30% to 80%, and the frontier re-sorts in an animated shuffle. 'The Corroboration Illusion: When More News Makes LLM Forecasts Less True' (arXiv 2609.22246, Sept 2026) jumps to the top: it is the free 25-minute item most likely to move them down. The AIA Forecaster report (2511.07678) sinks, because at 80% it is already priced in. Six days later the Sunday lamp sweeps the front row. Nine of fourteen cards fade to dusty grey, and the reliability curve draws itself well below the diagonal: 'Your 70% means 29%.'
screens: Setup: questions with credence sliders, weekly budget, access holdings
Inbox triage strip with keyboard hints, Evidence Pre-reads, hour estimates and access chips
Frontier scatter (hours vs expected shift; chapters and papers as separate dots) with budget line, risk slider and prior sliders
The desk: three depth bands, user piles beside landmarks, dust and a capacity meter; AR passthrough mock
Post-read log: new credence, computed log-odds shift, note; question sparklines annotated by item
Sunday sweep: lamp pass, reliability diagrams, recommender calibration, signal-value table, stale questions
Monday plan card with page-level deep links, routes, total cost and calendar export
Phone fallback: an honest grouped list
candidates.data_needed:
Sources:
- papers.json: 1,457 abstracts with dates and themes.
- catalog.json: pp for hours; acc and ia for routes; call numbers.
- openstax.json.
- Open Library TOCs with page numbers for the top ~1,500 works, fetched at build.
- Gutenberg chapter headings parsed from the full texts.
- Unpaywall, for DOIs.

Precomputed:
- Pre-reads for three demo questions, over about 200 items each.
- One-line takeaways for every paper.
- A clearly labelled demo persona with 8 weeks of synthetic history for the calibration screens.

Persistence: per-user rows in the db capability (itemId, x, band, p, placedAt, openedAt, readAt, credences); on the wiki, localStorage plus JSON export.

Weekly arrivals: a scheduled Claude task can write each Monday's new arrivals into the in-tray via ArtifactData, so the artifact never needs a network call at runtime.
candidates.generation_role:
On the fly:
- Evidence Pre-reads as structured JSON: relevance, direction, 10/50/90 shift, crux, grade, and a rationale citing an abstract sentence. They are batched about 30 per call, generated lazily for the ~20 items nearest the frontier, and cached by (item, question, credence bucket).
- Bibliography parsing.
- Choosing which chapters of a TOC bear on which question.
- The dust gists.

Claude never places a card.

Deterministic: the knapsack, frontier, routes, Bayes arithmetic and all calibration maths.

Fallback: precomputed pre-reads for the demo questions. Otherwise a heuristic score (theme overlap × recency × access cost) with wide intervals, labelled 'no AI pre-read', and a regex citation parser.
candidates.prior_art:
- Value-of-information analysis (Howard; Raiffa & Schlaifer) and QURI's Squiggle.
- Personal forecast tracking: Fatebook, PredictionBook, Metaculus.
- Reading queues and recommenders: Readwise Reader and Zotero queues, Scholar Inbox's per-user model, arxiv-sanity.
- Spatial layout: Data Mountain (Robertson et al., UIST 1998), Cockburn & McKenzie (CHI 2002) on depth hurting retrieval, and BumpTop piles.
- Karnofsky's review-first reading.

None of these combine units at chapter level, an hours budget, value measured as credence shift, access routing and scored calibration.
candidates.risks:
- Noisy early estimates: LLM-estimated update sizes will be badly calibrated at first. The ledger exists to measure this, but early rankings will be noisy.
- Goodhart: expected update favours contrarian or sensational items, so weight by evidence grade.
- Fatigue: over-quantification has to cost under 10 minutes a week.
- Self-report: 'read' is self-reported; opened-link tracking is the honest proxy.
- Question quality: vague questions make shifts meaningless, so require resolvable phrasing.
- Coverage: TOCs are patchy, so many units fall back to whole books flagged 'no TOC', and IA deep links can land a few pages off.
- Sign-in: db needs a signed-in viewer.
- Honesty: the demo persona must never pose as the reader's real log.

usefulness.why: It directly attacks 'too much to read', and its weekly arXiv triage plus an hours-budget knapsack fits this reader's Bayesian habits. But value-of-information ranking depends on noisy LLM shift estimates and a disciplined question-tracking ritual, and much of the reader's reading is field-understanding rather than resolving 3-8 questions. The desk, AR and Sunday-lamp parts add overhead, not usefulness.

novelty.why: Ranking chapters and papers by expected credence shift per hour, dragging a prior to re-sort the frontier, and then scoring the recommender's own calibration are unusual and suit a forecaster. It is still a reading planner, the desk is Data Mountain, and its core overlaps with Evidence Ledger.

demo.why: Its value appears only across weeks of use, so the calibration and Sunday-sweep screens must run on a synthetic persona. Chapter-level dots need TOCs we don't have, and it has more than 8 subsystems. Only the frontier scatter with a credence drag is a convincing one-day piece.

candidates.name: Lights Out in the Stacks
candidates.tagline: Every work shelved in true call-number order in a dark building. Your query is a lamp, the books that discuss it turn fore-edge-out to show the exact pages, and the shelves reshelve themselves by any principle you type.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) The building.
- 6,518 LC-classed catalog works stand in exact lcc sort order; 29,007 Gutenberg books are shelved at class level.
- 1,457 arXiv papers are thin pamphlet boxes, placed by a ~10-row theme-to-LCC table: alignment papers at Q334.7 beside Russell's Human Compatible, forecasting papers at HB3730 beside Tetlock's Superforecasting, scholarly-search papers in Z beside Gleick's The Information.
- Spine thickness comes from page count. Binding follows era: gilt cloth before 1920, jackets 1950-1990, glossy paperback after.
- A dot at the foot of each spine, like a bookseller's price sticker, shows access: green public/Gutenberg, blue borrowable, amber print-disabled only, grey none.
- Range end-panels carry real captions from lcc-outline.json ('QA273-QA280 Probabilities. Mathematical statistics'). There is a minimap of LC classes and a call-number jump box.
2) Lights out. Type a query or pick a subject heading. The house lights dim and every matching spine glows, brighter for stronger matches. The minimap becomes a heat map, and a side strip counts the scatter: 'forecasting: 313 works across 51 LC subclasses: T 56, HD 24, HG 24, CB 20, Q 19, HB 15...'
3) Turn around. For terms in the precomputed Search Inside set, glowing books rotate 180 degrees in a staggered wave so their fore-edge faces you. Each hit page is a bright line at its relative depth in the book. A tight band means a chapter on the topic, scattered lines mean passing mentions, and a dark shelf means nobody there discusses it. A toggle shows the same data as a TileBars matrix (books x page deciles).
4) Pull. Click a glow and the camera dollies down the aisle; unlit neighbours stay visible. Hovering pulls a book half out, showing its first sentence, editions, reading-log count and call number. Clicking flies it to a lectern with:
- a riffle strip of hit pages with snippets;
- readable pages, for public-domain books;
- an access router for each page.
5) Halos and threads.
- A warm glow covers the pulled book's shelf neighbours. A ceiling light-thread runs to its semantic neighbours in far bays.
- For about 400 hero works, red threads run to their strongest critics and blue threads to the books they build on. Each thread carries a one-line crux and an evidence-basis tag, and is dashed if it rests on metadata only.
- Press R to ride the red thread across the building.
6) Misshelf. In each bay you visit, one spine is turned backwards: a book from a distant class that Claude argues belongs here, with a handwritten slip. Example: Perrow's Normal Accidents (T54) in the Bayesian decision-analysis shelf.
7) Reshelve.
- Select a stretch, say the ~400 works from QA273 to QA279.5 plus BC logic and HB decision theory.
- Choose a fixed order (Dewey, first-publication year, reading-log popularity, edition count) or type a principle: 'by school of probability', 'by how much math it assumes', 'by which decision it would help me make', or 'by stance on: can expert forecasters be trusted?' (the debate aisle).
- Claude proposes 4-9 aisles with editable definitions, then assigns books in batches of 50 with a confidence for each.
- Spines animate into labelled aisles. Low-confidence books land on a sorting cart. Each aisle gets a shelf-talker that may only mention books on that aisle.
- 'Back to LC' flies everything home. Reshelvings are saved as named views.
8) Devices.
- Laptops, phones and the wiki default to a 2D StackLife-style call-number ribbon.
- Desktop offers the 3D aisle.
- 'Enter stacks' starts WebXR on a headset, from the wiki URL: a true-scale aisle where you pull books with a controller.
candidates.why_clever:
A ranked list removes the most valuable thing a library has: a century of decisions about what belongs next to what.
- Lighting a query inside the classification shows three things in one glance: where a subject clusters, where it is scattered (forecasting splits across technology, finance, civilization, statistics and psychology), and the unsearched neighbours of every hit. Those neighbours are where shelf serendipity comes from; McKay, Smith & Chang found that a book whose shelf neighbour was borrowed is far more likely to be borrowed.
- The fore-edge adds the one thing only digital search provides, page-level location inside in-copyright books without their text, for 300 books at once.
- Reshelving makes the classification itself something to question: Warburg's 'law of the good neighbour' on demand.
- Critic threads show the adjacency classification hides most, which is disagreement.
- Access colour makes the price of a field visible: the Bayesian shelf at QA279.5 is almost entirely print-disabled or has no ebook.
candidates.signature_moment: The house lights go out and the reader types 'forecasting'. The building lights up in islands: a bright bay at QA280 (Box & Jenkins, Harvey), a glow at CB158 (Silver's The Signal and the Noise), a flicker at HB3730 (Superforecasting), and a drift of arXiv pamphlet boxes beside it. They fly to the brightest island, and every glowing book turns fore-edge-out with a soft clack, gold lines marking exactly which pages discuss the topic. They pull Superforecasting. Its red thread snaps taut across three aisles, and pressing R rides it to Fooled by Randomness (HG4521). A crux card hangs there: 'What counts as a track record: short-horizon Brier scores, or survival in fat tails?'

Lights-out query: glowing spines, heat-map minimap, scatter histogram by LC subclass
Aisle at QA279.4-QA280 with legible spines and end-panel caption
Fore-edge wall mid-turn and lit, with the TileBars matrix toggle
Lectern: pulled book with a riffle strip of hit pages, snippets and an access router for each page

2D call-number ribbon fallback; WebXR aisle with controller ray
candidates.data_needed:
Source files: catalog.json (lcc, call, ddc, pp, y, acc, ia, ed, wtr, rl, fs, s); gutenberg.json (c, s, b); papers.json (th mapped to LCC anchors); lcc-outline.json.

Precompute:
- Normalised LC sort keys, fixing forms like 'Q -0375.00000000.T35', plus an 'unshelved cart' for unclassified works.
- Bay, range and shelf coordinates.
- A MiniSearch/FlexSearch index over titles, subjects, bookshelves and abstracts.
- A fiction filter (PZ/PR/PS).
- Dewey and year orderings.
- Search Inside hits for about 25-50 seed terms, normalised by the scanned edition's page count (~0.5 MB).
- The top 20 semantic neighbours of each work (~0.6 MB).
- Critic and builds-on edges, plus thesis sentences, for about 400 hero works, each with evidence basis and confidence.
- About 40 misshelf slips.
- Reshelvings for 4-5 principles over 3 stretches.

Rendering: three.js instanced meshes, with text drawn only near the camera.
candidates.prior_art:
- Virtual shelf browsers: Harvard Library Innovation Lab's StackLife/ShelfLife (spine size from page count, usage heat; now offline), Open Library Explorer (3D shelves by LCC/DDC, 2020), Stanford SearchWorks virtual shelf.
- Research prototypes: Blended Shelf (Konstanz, CHI 2013), Bohemian Bookshelf (Thudt, Hinrichs & Carpendale, CHI 2012), Hearst's TileBars, Card, Robertson & York's WebBook (1996).
- Older ideas: Aby Warburg's library, Ranganathan's faceted Colon Classification, Kialo, and medieval fore-edge shelving.

New here: a query lit across the whole building; fore-edge page hits for in-copyright books; papers shelved as pamphlets; generated misshelves; reshelving by any principle; and critic threads.
candidates.risks:
- Catalog noise: subject queries pulled in The Firm and Harry Potter, so a fiction filter is needed. About 8% of works are unclassified, and Gutenberg records carry only class letters.
- Search Inside limits: it covers only IA-scanned editions, page_num may be a scan leaf, and only precomputed terms work inside the artifact.
- Reshelving quality and speed: assignments are only as good as thin metadata, and about 400 books take ~8 batched calls and 20-40 s, so animate progressively.
- Critic edges for in-copyright books rest on metadata and model knowledge, not text, so tag the evidence basis and dash them.
- Navigation: 3D is slower than a list, so the 2D ribbon and minimap teleport carry the everyday value.
- WebXR likely won't run inside the claude.ai iframe.
- The arXiv-to-LCC mapping must be labelled 'shelved by Open Stacks'.
merged_from: Fore-Edge: the stacks that turn around

usefulness.why: Lighting a query across LC classes does reveal scatter and shelf neighbours. But 3D navigation is slower than a list, and the useful parts (fore-edge page hits, neighbours, access colour) are delivered better by Page Flags and a 2D ribbon. Mostly a vision piece.

novelty.why: 3D call-number shelves already exist (Open Library Explorer, and StackLife before it went offline), which caps the novelty. The new layers are strong: a query lights the whole building, books turn fore-edge-out to show page hits in in-copyright books, Claude reshelves by any principle you type, and generated misshelf slips add serendipity.

demo.why: The lit-islands screenshot would be spectacular, but legible 3D spines for 6.5k works in three.js plus fore-edge turns, threads and reshelving is not a one-day build. The fore-edge payoff is weak on our data because Search Inside returns about one page per lending book, so a 'tight band = chapter' rarely appears. The 2D ribbon is the feasible core.

candidates.name: Epoch Slider
candidates.tagline: Ask a question and drag a year from 1700 to 2026. The shelves fill, the idea's river widens across disciplines, and the answer rewrites itself to what the library could have told you then, with anachronisms caught by the corpus itself.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) The room. A year dial controls a reading room whose shelves hold only works first published by that year. Dates come from catalog first-publish years (with a date-confidence field), Gutenberg original dates resolved at build time, and arXiv dates. The room changes by era: gaslight, Carnegie-library oak, 1970s fluorescent, 2026 screen glow.
2) Shelf growth. Drag the dial and the shelves fill. QA279.5 (Bayesian statistics) grows from 1 book in the 1960s to 26 in the 2000s, matching real catalog counts. Margin labels mark arrivals: Lindley's Making Decisions (1971), Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis (1995), McElreath (2015). The arXiv forecasting papers drift in after 2015. A public-domain line (pre-1931, as of 2026) makes every shelf to its left glow green.
3) The river. Above the dial, the question's key terms render as a streamgraph:
- x is the year; lanes are LC classes (B, BC, BF, HA, HB, QA, Q335, T).
- Width is the number of works using the term, counted from Gutenberg full texts, catalog subjects and first sentences, and arXiv abstracts.
- Coloured strands within the river are senses, which Claude infers from about 60 keyword-in-context (KWIC) lines. 'Calibration' splits into instrument calibration, forecaster calibration (meteorology and Brier 1950) and model calibration (papers.json mentions rise from 3 in 2013 to 67 in 2026).
- A shaded band over roughly 1929-1990 marks years when full texts are in copyright and only metadata counts.
- 'Before the word' extends the river backward through earlier phrasings: 'inverse probability' before 'Bayesian', Galton's 'vox populi' before 'wisdom of crowds'.
- Click a strand to open its concordance drawer.
4) Ask. Claude answers as of the chosen year. Its tools (search_catalog, grep_text, search_papers) enforce year ≤ dial on the page side, so later works can't be retrieved. Every claim must cite a work from that period: a verified quote for public-domain text, metadata only for in-copyright books.
5) Scrub. With a question pinned, dragging the dial re-renders the brief as a redline diff. Each insertion is tagged with the book that made it possible ('new in 1961: Raiffa & Schlaifer, Applied Statistical Decision Theory').
6) Anachronism linter. A dated lexicon built from the corpus underlines terms in two colours. Red: the term appears in no source up to the cutoff. Amber: the term appears but in a different sense, with period KWIC lines as evidence. Claude can rewrite the brief in period vocabulary, and the linter shows the first year the shelf could support a concept ('Brier score': not before 1950).
7) Hindsight and retro-forecasts. Later sources are hidden by default; a 'what happened next' toggle reveals them. In retro-forecast mode you forecast as a reader in year Y would have, then the outcome is revealed and you get a Brier score.
8) Reading lists. Any era's shelf exports as a reading list, e.g. 'the scholar's shelf, 1921': about 150 works, nearly all free.
candidates.why_clever:
Search engines flatten time. The slider turns the catalog's date field into an instrument.
- You can watch a literature grow, see when a question became answerable, and see which specific books moved the answer: a view of intellectual progress that needs no citation data.
- Year-capped retrieval is the same no-leakage discipline that forecasting backtests need, so it doubles as hindsight-bias training.
- The river shows how ideas moved across disciplines and renamings. It often reveals that a 'new' AI-evaluation problem is an old probability problem in a new lane.
- The copyright band makes corpus bias visible instead of interpolating over it.
- The linter lets the corpus check the model: a cheap deterministic test for generated history's most common failure, projecting modern concepts backward.
- The public-domain line shows exactly what share of an answer free texts can support.
candidates.signature_moment: The question is 'Can reasoning be done by a machine?' At 1854, Boole's An Investigation of the Laws of Thought appears, and the brief talks of an algebra of thought. At 1874, Jevons's The Principles of Science enters with his Logical Machine. Claude's draft calls it 'an early computer', and the linter underlines 'computer' in amber. In every source up to 1874 the word means a person, as when Jevons describes the logarithm tables 'worked out by a staff of sixty or eighty computers, most of whom were acquainted only with the rules of arithmetic'. The brief rewrites itself to 'a reasoning machine'. Drag on through Wiener's Cybernetics (1948), Hofstadter (1979) and Bostrom (2014). At 2026, two hundred arXiv alignment papers flood the Q335 lane of the river, and the green public-domain line slides past with a note: 'Everything you read before 1931 is free.'

Shelf-growth animation: QA279.5 filling decade by decade with labelled arrivals
River over the dial: LC lanes, sense strands with glosses, copyright band, concordance drawer
Period answer with verified quotes and the books it drew from
Redline diff between two years, with the enabling book shown on each insertion
Anachronism linter: red absent terms, amber sense drift with period KWIC, first supportable year
Retro-forecast and hindsight toggle
Era shelf as a reading list; date audit of low-confidence works
candidates.data_needed:
Dates:
- catalog.json y is noisy (Meditations is dated 1626 and the Bible 1200). Add a date-confidence field and sanity-check against Wikidata where a wd id exists.
- gutenberg.json y is the year a book was added, so original years must be resolved at build from Open Library matches, Wikidata or author dates.
- papers.json dates; true years for the local texts from texts/index.json.

Build:
- 500-1,000 public-domain nonfiction texts from Gutenberg in B, BC, BF, HA, HB, QA, Q and T.
- KWIC entries for about 200 epistemics terms (term, work, year, line, 160-character context), 5-15 MB in shards.
- A dated lexicon: for each term, the earliest year it appears in the corpus's text, titles, subjects or first sentences, with period KWIC samples.
- Year-filtered TF-IDF indexes for each era.

Precomputed: answers and diffs for about 8 questions × 6 eras; senses and bridges for 12 showcase terms.
candidates.prior_art:
- Term frequency over time: Google Books Ngram Viewer and Culturomics (Michel et al. 2011); HathiTrust+Bookworm; Voyant Tools.
- Semantic change: Hamilton, Leskovec & Jurafsky (2016) on diachronic word embeddings; the OED's first-citation dates.
- Visualisation and citation history: streamgraphs (Byron & Wattenberg 2008); HistCite.
- Reconstructions of historical libraries (Newton's, Darwin's).
- Period-locked language models such as MonadGPT.
- ForecastBench leakage controls and knowledge-cutoff backtests.
- Fienberg (2006), 'When Did Bayesian Inference Become Bayesian?'
candidates.risks:
- The cutoff governs sources, not the model. Claude knows what happened next and can leak it through framing. The linter catches vocabulary, not ideas, so frame the output as 'what this shelf supports'.
- Dates are noisy: reprints and translations (the Gutenberg Laplace is a 1902 translation of the 1814 essay).
- Coverage is uneven: before 1900 it relies on Gutenberg, the mid-century is thin and must be shown honestly, and arXiv starts in 1991.
- The earliest occurrence in this corpus is not the earliest in history.
- Sense clustering on small samples is unstable.
- 'Resemblance' bridges can imply influence that didn't exist.
- The public-domain line follows US law.

usefulness.why: Watching a shelf grow and linting anachronisms are intellectually delightful history-of-ideas exercises. They don't address finding, accessing or prioritising reading, and noisy dates plus thin mid-century coverage limit trust.

novelty.why: I know of no tool that does what this does. Retrieval is capped at the dial's year, so the brief rewrites itself as a redline, each insertion tagged with the book that made it possible. The anachronism linter lets the corpus police the model (the 'computer' moment). Ngram Viewer, diachronic embeddings and MonadGPT each do only part of this.

demo.why: Gutenberg's y field is the year a book was added and catalog years are noisy, so original dates must be rebuilt first. The dated lexicon needs 500-1,000 texts, and sense strands need model clustering. The shelf-growth animation is easy, but the brief, the linter and the river need heavy precompute. The 'computer' anachronism example does check out in Jevons.

candidates.name: The Round Reading Room
candidates.tagline: All ~37,600 works on one cylindrical wall, with call number running around you and publication year rising to the ceiling. Labels sharpen from class names to sentences as you approach, and a whispered passage ripples up through time to every later work that took it up.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) The room. You stand at the centre of a round room in three.js, modelled on the British Museum's Round Reading Room (mouse-look on desktop, WebXR on a headset).
- Azimuth is LC call-number order: A at the door, running clockwise to Z.
- Height is first-publication year: about 1600 at the floor, about 1990 at eye level, 2026 at the ceiling.
- Each work is one instanced tile: 7,127 Open Library works; 29,007 Gutenberg books, dated by author life dates and shown as a band; 1,457 arXiv papers, mapped cs.AI to Q334-336, stat to QA276-279, econ to HB, cs.DL/cs.HC to Z.
- Colour shows access; tile size shows reading-log count.
2) Semantic zoom. As you walk toward the wall, labels change resolution, not just size:
- From across the room: 21 class bands lettered on the floor ring, each with a one-phrase gist.
- Closer: subclasses with counts and decade histograms.
- Closer still: call-number ranges with one-line summaries ('QA273-279.5: 317 books, from Ross's and Mendenhall's textbooks to Gelman's, McElreath's and Kruschke's Bayesian turn').
- At arm's length: titles, then one-line gists with access badges.
An altimeter shows the current power of ten. Typography marks provenance: roman for catalog metadata, italic with an AI tick for generated summaries, serif for verbatim text. Clicking any summary shows exactly what it covers.
3) Subject lamps and constellations. Choose 'decision making' and every tile carrying it lights up across BF448, HD30, QA279 and T57. Threads tie together topics that LCC scatters; forecasting sits at CB158, HB3730, HD30.6, HD61, JC328.2, Q375 and BF441.
4) The desk. Clicking a tile flies the book to a central desk modelled on Data Mountain, where pulled books keep their positions.
- A Gutenberg book opens as a riffle (a page strip with legible headings). The zoom continues down to the TOC with page heat, then paragraph gists, then verbatim sentences.
- An in-copyright book opens to its cover, TOC and an access-router card.
5) Ask the librarian. Claude has search_catalog and a light_trail(ids, captions) tool. Asked 'Where do I start on the history of Bayesian thought?', it draws a glowing trail across the wall in reading order, with a caption at each stop. Dwell on a wedge and it writes a bookstore-style 'shelf-talker' card.
6) Whisper. Select a passage at the desk and whisper it.
- Claude extracts an editable idea fingerprint, a set of terms and paraphrases: 'rule of succession', 'probability the sun rises', '(n+1)/(n+2)', 'uniform prior'.
- It queries catalog subjects and first sentences, Search Inside hits, abstracts and the other full texts.
- A ripple climbs the wall from the passage's year. Every tile that 'hears' the idea lights up, coloured by its relation to the passage, judged from its evidence snippet: restates, extends, critiques, applies or reframes.
- Faint dashed echo arcs propose a genealogy. Dark stretches show silences, and corpus coverage per decade is shown so a silence isn't mistaken for absence.
7) Unroll. The cylinder flattens into a 2D strata chart (x = call number with a Furnas fisheye, y = year) that zooms with the same changing labels. This is the everyday view on laptops, phones and the static wiki. Whispers render there as a swimlane echo plot (year x relation).
candidates.why_clever:
- Two meaningful axes let every item be shown at once. The classification axis brings back the stacks' adjacency and serendipity; the time axis shows how fields were born and aged.
- A 360-degree wall gives far more surface than a laptop and uses peripheral vision, which is where a headset actually beats a screen.
- Semantic zoom makes surveying and reading the same object at different magnifications, so there is no switch of tools between 'what's on this shelf?' and 'show me the page'. It rests on a recursive summary tree, the method Wu et al. (2021) used to summarise whole books, extended upward to shelves and classes.
- The whisper shows the temporal shape of an idea (bursts, silences, revivals, critiques) across books and papers. Citation graphs miss this, because ideas travel through books for centuries without formal citations.
A chat answer is a list. Here the answer is a path through space you can walk and remember.
candidates.signature_moment: You turn to the Q wedge and look up. Near the ceiling, Superintelligence (Q335), Human Compatible, The Alignment Problem and Life 3.0 (Q334.7) sit shoulder to shoulder in amber and grey. Low on the BC and QA wedges glow green Boole's Laws of Thought (#15114), Venn's Logic of Chance (#57359) and Keynes's Treatise on Probability (#32625): the ancestors are free tonight, while the descendants are on hold. Then you whisper Laplace's 'a bet of 1826214 to one that it will rise again to-morrow'. The ripple leaves 1814 and crosses sixty dark years. Jevons flares, Venn flashes red (a critique), Russell's chicken glows (a reframing). A long dim arc follows, then a burst of gold just under the ceiling: 2020s papers on calibration, base rates and LLM forecasters. Two hundred years of an argument light up in eight seconds.

Q wedge: AI-safety cluster near the ceiling, 19th-century logic and probability founders near the floor
Semantic zoom sequence: class band to range summary to gists, with altimeter and provenance inspector
Subject lamp 'decision making' lit across BF, HD, QA and T, with constellation threads
Desk: pulled books, one open in riffle view, one in-copyright book with TOC and access router
Librarian trail with numbered captions and a side panel streaming Claude's reasoning
Whisper: fingerprint card, ripple mid-flight with year counter, lit wall with relation colours, echo arcs and silences
Unrolled strata view with a fisheye at QA273 (a dozen 'Introduction to Probability' textbooks side by side) and the swimlane echo plot; headset mode

Sources:
- catalog.json: lcc, call, y, acc, rl, pp, ia, s, fs.
- gutenberg.json: c and s, plus original dates. Its y field is the year the book was added to Gutenberg, so rerun fetch-gutenberg.mjs keeping author life dates from pg_catalog.csv.

- Class-band boundaries.
- Inverted lists for the top 500 subjects.
- A summary tree: about 300 range summaries and 7,000 one-line gists. Batch generation at small-model prices costs well under $10.
- Paginated text for about 200 Gutenberg books in B, BC, HB, Q, QA and QH.
- Open Library TOCs for the top ~1,000 works.
- int8 384-dim embeddings for the ~8,600 non-Gutenberg items (~3.3 MB), plus neighbour lists.
- 12 canned trails and about 40 shelf-talkers.
- 5 complete whispers: Laplace's sunrise; Hume's 'Custom, then, is the great guide of human life'; Venn's frequency definition; Darwin's 'struggle for existence'; Mill's harm principle.
