Live:
- Librarian trails via light_trail, with ids validated.
- Shelf-talkers.
- Gists and range summaries for regions that lack them, generated as they come into view.
- Whispers: fingerprint extraction, query expansion into the corpus vocabulary, and relation labels plus a one-line 'how it echoes' for the top ~40 candidates. These use snippet evidence only and are labelled 'suggested'.

Precomputed: layout, lamps, riffle pages, the summary tree, canned trails and the five whispers.

Fallback on the wiki: canned trails, keyword lamps and precomputed summaries. A custom whisper falls back to lexical matching on the passage's rare terms, with all tiles white and no relation colours.
candidates.prior_art:
- The room and its views: the British Museum Round Reading Room; StackLife; Mackinlay, Robertson & Card's Perspective Wall (1991); WebBook/WebForager (1996); Data Mountain (1998); Furnas's fisheye views.
- Zoom: the Eameses' Powers of Ten (1977); Pad++ and zoomable user interfaces (Perlin & Fox 1993; Bederson & Hollan 1994); Nelson's StretchText and Telescopic Text; Wu et al. 2021 on recursive book summarisation.
- Tracing ideas: Google Books Ngram Viewer; scite citation intents; the Viral Texts project; Börner's maps of science.
candidates.risks:
- Year proxies for Gutenberg works are rough, so show a band, not a point.
- About 650 works lack LC call numbers and need an 'unshelved cart'.
- Legibility of 37k tiles: labels must appear only on approach, and text atlases need care.
- WebXR may be blocked in the artifact iframe, so desktop mouse-look and the 2D unroll must stand alone.
- Summaries are lossy, and relation labels read from snippets are error-prone. Show the evidence, and keep echo arcs faint and dashed.
- The catalog is popularity-weighted, so a silence may only mean 'not in our 7k'.
- Novelty over utility: the unroll is the everyday tool, and the room is the overview.

usefulness.why: An impressive overview spectacle, but a 37k-tile cylinder and whisper ripples rarely help decide what to read or find a page. The 2D strata unroll is the only part likely to see repeat use, and even that overlaps with other concepts.

novelty.why: It puts all 37k works on one call-number × year cylinder. Semantic zoom runs from class bands down to sentences, built on a recursive summary tree. The 'whisper' ripples a passage through two centuries with relation colours, and no product traces an idea's temporal shape across books like that. Its parts (StackLife, Perspective Wall, Powers of Ten) are old, and there is real risk of spectacle over use.

demo.why: A cylinder of 37k coloured tiles is cheap and striking, but everything that makes it clever has to be canned in a day: semantic zoom over 7k generated gists, whisper relation labelling, and re-dating Gutenberg works. It would be a wow screenshot with a hollow interior.

candidates.name: Synteny
candidates.tagline: A genome browser for courses and textbooks. Align a 30-hour lecture series against its textbook in one dot plot, line up books from 1814 to 2024 like chromosomes, and turn every lecture into chapters you can riffle.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Pick a pairing or a lineage.
- Pairings:
  - MIT 6.041SC Probabilistic Systems Analysis (Tsitsiklis; OCW transcripts) with Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis's Introduction to Probability (QA273 .B554). The book has no ebook in the catalog, so it sits unlit, with a library or buy route, beside free OpenStax alternatives.
  - MIT 18.06 with Strang's Introduction to Linear Algebra.
  - Harvard Stat 110 with Blitzstein & Hwang (free PDF).
  - MacKay's Cambridge lectures with Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (free PDF).
- Lineage 'Probability, 1814-2024':
  - full-text tracks for Laplace, Jevons, Venn, Poincaré and Keynes;
  - CC BY tracks for OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, Statistics, and Principles of Data Science;
  - TOC-only tracks for Ross, Gelman et al. and McElreath.
2) Lectures become chapters. Transcripts are cut into 'boards', one per definition, theorem, worked example or warning the lecturer states, each with a timestamp. This yields a generated lecture TOC ('L14 12:30-28:00: Conditional expectation as a random variable'). The course joins the catalog as a free 'book', so the Bindery and the Portfolio can pick segments from it.
3) Dot plot. The x-axis is the whole course as continuous time, with lecture ticks. The y-axis is the book's sections, with chapter bands. Each dot is a roughly 2-minute transcript window placed at its best-matching section and shaded by match strength.
- A diagonal means the course follows the book.
- Off-diagonal blocks are reorderings.
- Horizontal empty bands are sections never lectured.
- Vertical stripes are lecture material the book lacks.
4) Brush a region. The transcript excerpt and the book section appear side by side: the text where the book is free, otherwise the page range and access route. A 'jump to 34:12' link plays the video embedded on the wiki and links out from the artifact.
5) Watch-or-read strip. For each section it shows whether the lecture or the book covers it more fully, so the reader can build a mixed path (watch §2.3, read §2.4).
6) Synteny tracks. Each book is a horizontal track scaled 0-100%, with chapter blocks. Sections are tagged from a vocabulary of about 150 concepts with an alias table. Ribbons join the same concept across tracks, and crossing ribbons show reorderings. An events panel lists four kinds of concept:
- conserved: present in every track;
- lost: present in the 19th-century lineage but absent from modern textbooks, e.g. the credibility of testimony;
- renamed: the same idea under a new term;
- novel: appears only after some date, e.g. the bootstrap.
7) Synopsis view. Click a ribbon to see one column per book, laid out like a Gospel synopsis. Each column shows that book's treatment: the verbatim passage, position (%), pages devoted, prerequisites assumed, notation ('P(A|B)' vs 'the chance of'), motivating example (urn, die, sunrise, mortality table, medical test), and stance (frequency vs degree of belief). Phrases shared between columns are colour-coded. 'Learn it from this one' routes to that exact section.
8) Amphitheatre (headset). Boards fill raked tiers, lecture by lecture. A course scrubber replays the semester as a time-lapse, with chalk lines snapping between boards that depend on each other. Ask a question and the boards Claude's answer cites glow around the hall. On desktop and phone, a flat board grid (lecture x order) replaces the hall.
candidates.why_clever:
Two mature traditions already solved the problem of 'same material, different order and wording'.
- Dot plots have shown how two long sequences correspond, in one picture, since Gibbs & McIntyre (1970).
- Synopses have aligned parallel texts since Griesbach (1776).
Nobody applies them to courses and textbooks, yet that is exactly the problem of indexing lectures by transcript and treating them as chapters.
- A 30-hour course becomes navigable at a glance: gaps and reorderings jump out.
- The reader can swap media section by section, which makes video, the least skimmable medium, something you can riffle.
- Across books, synteny shows an idea's institutional history: what was dropped, reordered or renamed between 1814 and 2024.
- The synopsis shows which treatment suits your prerequisites.
candidates.signature_moment: The 6.041 versus Bertsekas-Tsitsiklis matrix renders as a clean diagonal staircase, except for one bright block sitting off it. You click the block, the transcript scrolls to the exact minute where the lecturer jumps ahead to a later chapter's idea, and the book pane shows that section's page range and its access route. Then you switch to the lineage and select 'rule of succession'. A ribbon runs bright through Laplace's sunrise bet, Jevons's inverse method and Venn's chapter-long attack, then stops dead at the OpenStax tracks, like a deleted gene.
screens: Pairing and lineage picker with access badges for each side
Dot-plot overview with lecture ticks, chapter bands and match shading
Brushed focus: transcript excerpt and book section side by side with a timestamp link
Gap report and watch-or-read strip with a mixed path
Generated lecture TOC: the course rendered as a book
Synteny tracks with concept ribbons, crossings and events panel (conserved / lost / renamed / novel)
Synopsis columns for one concept with shared phrases colour-coded
Amphitheatre: hall of boards in a mid-semester time-lapse, a question with its cited boards glowing; flat board-grid fallback
candidates.data_needed:
Transcripts:
- MIT OCW 6.041SC and 18.06, fetched at build (CC BY-NC-SA; ocw.mit.edu returned 200).
- Stat 110 and MacKay, if obtainable.

Book structure:
- Full text of the free PDFs (Blitzstein-Hwang, MacKay's ITILA).
- Gutenberg texts: Laplace, Jevons, Venn and Poincaré, plus Keynes #32625 and Boole #15114.
- OpenStax section HTML (URLs in openstax.json).
- Open Library or publisher TOCs with page ranges for in-copyright books, plus Search Inside hits for alias terms.

Precompute:
- Board segmentation.
- Embeddings for 2-minute windows and for sections; TOC-only sections get Claude-written summaries to embed.
- A sparse similarity matrix (about 900 windows × 200 sections).
- The concept vocabulary and alias table.
- Section-to-concept tags (model-assisted, spot-checked by hand).
- N-gram overlap for shared phrasing, and normalised positions.
candidates.generation_role:
Precomputed with Claude at build time: boards, lecture TOC titles, section summaries for in-copyright TOCs, concept tags, and watch-or-read judgements.

Live:
- 'Explain this block': why the lecturer departed from the book, and what each source does better.
- A small one-off alignment of a pasted transcript against a chosen TOC.
- Finding a new concept across tracks via search_sections and get_section. The page renders verbatim text from section ids, so Claude never types a quote.
- Answers grounded in transcripts and free text, with board citations.
- A 3-sentence 'how these treatments differ'.

Fallback: everything precomputed still works, with keyword search across boards and no live explanations.
candidates.prior_art:
- Comparative genomics: dot plots and synteny viewers (Gibbs & McIntyre 1970; MUMmer, D-GENIES, Circos, SynVisio).
- Parallel texts: Gospel synopses (Griesbach 1776; Aland's Synopsis Quattuor Evangeliorum); the Syntopicon.
- Lecture indexing: ClassTranscribe, Video Digests, Panopto search; MIT OpenCourseWare.
- Other: Hearst's TileBars; Metacademy; Open Syllabus; 'The Reconstruction of Science Phylogeny' (arXiv 0904.3154).
candidates.risks:
- Transcripts: availability and licensing outside OCW are uncertain. YouTube captions are often unfetchable, and CC BY-NC-SA blocks commercial reuse.
- Maths: mathematical lectures embed poorly ('this times that' versus notation), and much is written on the board but never said.
- Video can't play inside the artifact.
- Tagging: quality depends on concept tags and on alias recall for old vocabulary ('chance', 'inverse method').
- Unverified events: the 'lost' and 'renamed' claims are hypotheses to verify against fetched texts. One example is the rule of succession resurfacing as add-one smoothing in ML.
- Scope: books of very different scope need normalisation.
- Effort: only 2-4 pairings are realistic, so this is a deep mockup with one genuinely computed alignment, and the OpenStax fetch is the heaviest build step.

usefulness.why: Lecture-versus-textbook alignment and watch-or-read paths help when learning a technical subject from a course. That is a few times a year at most, and only 2-4 pairings are realistically buildable. The lineage and amphitheatre parts are history-of-textbooks curiosities.

novelty.why: It borrows genome dot plots and synteny tracks to align a lecture course against its textbook, and books from 1814 to 2024 against each other. 'Rule of succession' stopping dead at OpenStax like a deleted gene is a picture nobody has drawn. The ambition is high and only 2-4 pairings are realistic, but the idea is a genuine first.

demo.why: It needs transcript fetching and segmentation, plus an alignment against a textbook that is no_ebook (TOC only), so a clean diagonal is unlikely. Lineage concept-tagging across 8 books is a large build, and video can't play inside the artifact. This is the weakest one-day bet.

candidates.name: Prophecy Audit
candidates.tagline: Every dated prediction on the futurology shelf, extracted, resolved and Brier-scored, so you can sort the forecasters' books by how calibrated they turned out to be.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Open the Forecasts shelf. gutenberg.json already tags 'Twentieth century -- Forecasts':
- H. G. Wells, Anticipations (1901, #19229)
- T. Baron Russell, A Hundred Years Hence (1905, #48674)
- Robert Grimshaw, Fifty Years Hence: or, What May Be in 1943 (1892, #68096)
- Arthur Bird, Looking Forward (1899)
- Henry Hartshorne, 1931: A Glance at the Twentieth Century (1881)
- Pieter Harting, Anno Domini 2071
- more Wells: What Is Coming? (1916), A Year of Prophesying (1924), The Way the World Is Going (1928).
In-copyright futurology from the catalog sits on the same shelf, as metadata only: 144 'technological forecasting' and 22 'futurology' works, e.g. Clarke's Profiles of the Future (1962), Feigenbaum and McCorduck's The Fifth Generation (1983), Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014), Tegmark's Life 3.0 (2017).
2) Pick a book. Claude extracts checkable predictions chapter by chapter and streams them as cards. Each card has:
- the verbatim sentence, string-verified;
- an operationalised question in Metaculus style, with a resolution date;
- an implied probability, from the author's hedge word via Sherman Kent's 'Words of Estimative Probability' table ('almost certainly' about 93%, 'probably' about 75%, 'chances about even' 50%). Anticipations alone uses 'probably' 109 times.
3) Claude proposes a resolution (yes / no / ambiguous / too vague) with a dated evidence note. A human accepts or edits it.
4) The book is scored:
- Brier and log scores, and a calibration curve;
- boldness (mean distance from 50%);
- resolvability rate (share of 'predictions' that could be checked at all);
- timing error (early or late, in years).
5) Hindsight Test. You see a prediction with its resolution hidden and give your own P(came true). You are then scored against the author and the crowd, which exposes your own hindsight bias.
6) Author arc. Plot Wells across 1901, 1916, 1924 and 1928: did he get better?
7) Shelf mode re-sorts the spines by Brier score, boldness or resolvability.
candidates.why_clever:
Libraries shelve futurology by topic, never by track record, and nobody can read 30 books to check.
- Extracting, resolving and scoring predictions turns a shelf of claims into a dataset with base rates.
- It answers epistemics questions no search box can: how good were confident book-length forecasts, and do hedge words carry information?
- It gives a forecaster a long-range reference class with real quotes.
- The Hindsight Test is a calibration exercise built from history.
candidates.signature_moment: Wells, Anticipations, line 4528 streams in: '...long before the year A.D. 2000, and very probably before 1950, a successful aeroplane will have soared and come home safe and sound.' The page splits it into two nested predictions: P(by 2000), and P(by 1950) at 'very probably' (about 80%). Both resolve YES, in December 1903, two years after publication. The calibration chart marks Wells as right but underconfident on timing: 47 years early. Then the shelf animates, spines sliding into Brier order: Wells's technology chapters to the left, Grimshaw's 1943 utopia with its 'great air-ships' toward the right, and a grey 'mostly unresolvable' pile at the end.
screens: Shelf view: futurology spines (public-domain full text; in-copyright as metadata ghosts), sortable by Brier, boldness, resolvability or year; colour by score
Extraction stream: prediction cards with verified quote, operationalised question, hedge word and implied p, plus a 'not a prediction' veto
Resolution queue: Claude-proposed resolutions with evidence notes; accept, edit or mark ambiguous; the resolution policy shown
Book audit: prediction table, calibration curve, Brier decomposition (reliability, resolution), timing-error histogram
Hindsight Test game: hidden resolution, your probability, reveal, your Brier score against the author's
Author arc: one author's scores across books and years
Methodology: Kent WEP mapping, handling of ambiguity and fiction-framed books, sample sizes with CIs
candidates.data_needed:
- gutenberg.json subjects, to select about 20 forecast books. Full texts are fetched at build time; #19229, #48674 and #68096 were tested and download fine, at 0.1-0.5 MB each.
- catalog.json for the in-copyright futurology shelf: metadata only, plus predictions entered by the reader with page references.
- A Kent WEP lookup table.
- Precomputed: extracted, resolved predictions for 5 books, generated with Claude at build time. A human spot-checks the resolutions, which are stored with evidence notes and dates.
candidates.prior_art:
- Forecast track records: Tetlock, Expert Political Judgment (2005); Ascher, Forecasting: An Appraisal for Policy-Makers (1978, in catalog.json, an audit of past forecasts); Open Philanthropy on the feasibility of long-range forecasting (Muehlhauser, 2019); Dan Luu's 'Futurist prediction methods and accuracy' (2022); Kurzweil's self-graded prediction reviews.
- Hedge words: Sherman Kent, 'Words of Estimative Probability' (1964).
- Retro-futurism: Benford, The Wonderful Future That Never Was (2010, in the catalog).
- Metaculus question operationalisation.
candidates.risks:
- Resolution is contested and prone to hindsight bias, so disagreement among resolvers must be shown, not hidden.
- Selection effects: extraction may favour striking claims.
- Genre: old fiction-framed books (Grimshaw writes as if from 1943) blur prediction and satire, so tag genre.
- Mapping Edwardian prose onto the Kent scale is a strong assumption.
- Small n per book means wide CIs.
- Fairness to living authors: score public-domain books by default, and label in-copyright entries as contributed by readers.
- Generated resolutions may be confidently wrong about historical dates.

usefulness.why: Scoring Edwardian futurology is a fun one-off epistemics study the forecaster might read once. It is not a tool for deciding what to read, finding pages or getting access, so it belongs as a wiki analysis, not an app.

novelty.why: Scoring futurists' book-length predictions has been done by hand (Kurzweil gradings, Dan Luu's survey of futurist accuracy, Ascher 1978, and as I recall Arb Research's scoring of Asimov, Clarke and Heinlein; I couldn't confirm that last one because the web-search budget had run out). Automating extraction, mapping hedge words via Kent's table, and sorting a shelf by Brier score is clever but narrow, and it automates an existing study.

demo.why: It is narrow and the data is real: I fetched Gutenberg #19229, the aeroplane line is at line 4530, and 'probably' appears 111 times. The Brier-sorted shelf and calibration curve make a striking, on-theme screenshot for a forecaster. The binding constraint is hand-checking Claude's historical resolutions, which realistically caps the audit at 2-3 books in a day.

candidates.name: Sieve
candidates.tagline: Scatter/Gather revived: pour ~37,600 works through a sieve. At each step the piles you keep are re-sorted into nine finer piles, and Claude names them as they land.
candidates.core_interaction:
1) Start screen. Every item (books, Gutenberg, papers) is a dot on a precomputed 2D embedding map, divided into 9 Voronoi piles. Each pile shows a label, its 3 most typical titles, a count, an access stack-bar (free, borrowable, none) and an era sparkline. You can also type a 'seed' query that gathers matching piles in advance.
2) Gather. Click 2-3 piles, for example 'Probability & statistical inference' and 'Judgment and decision psychology'.
3) Scatter. Those ~3,100 dots animate into a fresh layout and are re-clustered in the browser into 9 new piles, using k-means on stored 32-dimensional vectors with a deterministic seed.
4) Claude labels the new piles live, streaming. For each pile the page sends the 25 most central titles and subjects, the sibling piles and the gather history. Claude returns a label, one line on what distinguishes the pile from its siblings, and 3 representative ids.
5) Repeat: 37k, then 3,100, then 420, then 60, then a final list. A left-hand 'sieve column' records the funnel as nested bars with labels and counts. The history works as an editable query: click any earlier level to branch from it.
6) Steer with words. Type 'more mathematical' or 'only things I can read free tonight'. Claude turns the nudge into calls to page tools, reweight(direction_terms) and filter(field, value), and the current set scatters again.
7) 'Road not taken' panel. Claude summarises what was in the piles you dropped at each step and offers one wildcard item from each, for deliberate serendipity.
8) The final pile becomes a reading list with access chips. Send it to the Portfolio, the Bindery or the Circulation Desk.
candidates.why_clever:
Search requires knowing the right words. Scatter/Gather lets you recognise rather than recall, which is how browsing in a bookstore works.
- The 1992 version failed mainly because its cluster labels were word salad. LLM labelling fixes exactly that weak link.
- Each step shows thousands of items as context but asks for one 9-way choice: an overview plus focus, at a human-sized decision cost.
- The funnel column makes the query an object you can inspect and branch, so you can see why you ended up where you did.
- The dropped-piles panel keeps the losing options visible.
- Books and papers finally sit in one pile.
candidates.signature_moment: Four clicks: Everything, then 'Uncertainty & inference', then 'Evaluating predictions', then 'Proper scoring rules and elicitation'. 37,000 dots collapse to 23, and the last label writes itself word by word. In the final pile, arXiv's 'Compatible Weighted Proper Scoring Rules' (1311.1131) and 'Calibration Scoring Rules for Practical Prediction Training' (1808.07501) sit beside Tetlock's Superforecasting and Annie Duke's Thinking in Bets: books and papers mixed in one pile at last.
screens: Overview: ~37k dots in 9 labelled Voronoi piles with access bars and era sparklines
Gather selection: 3 piles highlighted with a count of dots selected
Scatter animation mid-flight, then the new layout with labels streaming in
Sieve column: a 4-level funnel with branch points
Final pile as a reading list with access chips and send-to actions
Steer box: 'only free tonight' applied, green dots kept and the rest ghosted
Road-not-taken panel with summaries of dropped piles and wildcard picks
Offline state: precomputed labels for the top 2 levels and keyword labels below
candidates.data_needed:
Embeddings for all ~37,600 items, computed at build time with a local sentence-embedding model:
- Open Library works: title + subtitle + subjects + first sentence.
- arXiv: abstract.
- Gutenberg: subjects + bookshelves.
TF-IDF reduced by SVD is the fallback.

Also precomputed:
- A 2D UMAP layout.
- 32-dimensional PCA vectors quantised to int8 (~1.2 MB).
- A k-means hierarchy for 2 levels (9 + 81 piles), with Claude-written labels.
- An access field and year for each item.

Everything ships as one compact binary or JSON file next to the page. The layout is shared with the Bindery's map and Terra Incognita's semantic geography.
candidates.generation_role:
Live:
- Pile labels and the lines that distinguish each pile, for every new scatter (9 parallel short calls or one streamed JSON call).
- Turning steering text into reweight and filter tool calls.
- Road-not-taken summaries.

Precomputed: layout, vectors, and labels for the first two levels, so the first two clicks are instant everywhere.

Fallback: keyword labels from c-TF-IDF for deeper levels. Steering by text is disabled, but filters stay available as checkboxes.
candidates.prior_art:
- Scatter/Gather: Cutting, Karger, Pedersen & Tukey (SIGIR 1992) and Pirolli et al.'s user studies (1996).
- Topic and embedding maps: BERTopic, Nomic Atlas, and the Open Syllabus Galaxy (a UMAP of co-assignment embeddings over 1.1M titles).
- Clustering search engines: Grouper and Carrot2.
candidates.risks:
- Thin metadata for many Open Library works makes some clusters muddy.
- Item type can dominate clustering, with papers clumping apart from books. Normalise or weight by type.
- Labelling latency on each scatter needs streaming and good placeholders.
- k-means instability: seed deterministically, so the same gather gives the same piles.
- Readers may want search too; the typed seed covers that.

usefulness.why: Recognition-based drill-down with good LLM labels helps orient in an unfamiliar area and mixes books with papers. The reader would use it occasionally rather than weekly, and muddy clusters from thin Open Library metadata plus 29k mostly irrelevant Gutenberg titles will blunt it.

novelty.why: This is Scatter/Gather with LLM cluster labels, which Knowledge Navigator (2024) and Anthropic's Clio already did, on top of Nomic- and BERTopic-style maps. The road-not-taken panel is a small addition. It is worth building only as shared embedding and cluster infrastructure for the other concepts.

demo.why: Mechanically simple: k-means on int8 vectors in the browser, a d3-delaunay Voronoi layout and streamed labels. It needs a build-time embedding pipeline, and neither sklearn nor sentence-transformers is installed here. The 29k thin Gutenberg records will dominate the 'Everything' view, and the dot-atlas look is familiar from Nomic and Open Syllabus Galaxy.
